chapters.title: The Last Day
paragraphs: ECHECRATES: Were you there yourself, Phaedo, in the prison with Socrates on the day he drank the poison?
PHAEDO: Yes, Echecrates, I was there.

ECHECRATES: I'd love to hear about his death. What did he say in his last hours? We were told that he died by drinking poison, but nobody knew anything more — no one from Phlius travels to Athens these days, and it's been a long time since any stranger from Athens has come our way. So we never got a clear account.
PHAEDO: Didn't you hear about the trial either?
ECHECRATES: Yes, someone told us about the trial. But we couldn't understand why, after being condemned, he was put to death so long afterwards instead of at the time. Why was that?
PHAEDO: It was a coincidence, Echecrates. The stern of the ship the Athenians send to Delos happened to have been crowned with garlands the day before his trial.
ECHECRATES: What ship is this?

PHAEDO: It's the ship in which — according to Athenian tradition — Theseus once sailed to Crete, taking those fourteen young people with him, and saved them and himself. At the time, they're said to have vowed to Apollo that if they were saved, they would send a yearly pilgrimage to Delos. That custom still continues. From the moment the priest of Apollo crowns the stern of the ship, the whole period of the voyage to Delos and back is considered a sacred season, and during it the city is not allowed to be polluted by public executions. And when the ship is delayed by contrary winds, the time spent going and returning can stretch out a great deal. As I said, the ship was crowned on the day before the trial — and that is why Socrates lay in prison and wasn't put to death until long after his sentence.

ECHECRATES: And what was the manner of his death, Phaedo? What was said, what was done? Which of his friends were with him? Or did the authorities forbid them to be present, so that he had no friends near him when he died?
PHAEDO: No, several of them were with him.
ECHECRATES: If you have nothing else to do, I wish you'd tell me what happened — as exactly as you can remember.
PHAEDO: I have nothing at all to do, and I'll try to satisfy you. Being reminded of Socrates is always the greatest pleasure to me — whether I'm the one speaking about him, or someone else is.
ECHECRATES: You'll find that your listeners are of the same mind as you. And I hope you'll be as exact as you can.

PHAEDO: It was a strange feeling to be in his company. I could hardly believe I was watching the death of a friend, and so I didn't pity him, Echecrates. He died so fearlessly, and his words and his bearing were so noble and gracious, that to me he seemed blessed. I thought that in going to the other world he could not be without some divine call, and that he would be happy when he arrived there — if ever any man has been. That's why I didn't pity him in the way that might have seemed natural at such an hour. But I also didn't feel the pleasure I usually feel in philosophical conversation — and philosophy was the subject we were discussing. I was pleased, yet mixed into the pleasure there was a strange pain, because I kept reflecting that he was soon to die. This double feeling was shared by all of us. We were laughing and weeping by turns — especially the excitable Apollodorus. You know the sort of man he is?
ECHECRATES: Yes.
PHAEDO: He was completely beside himself, and I and all the rest of us were deeply moved.
ECHECRATES: Who was present?

PHAEDO: Of native Athenians, besides Apollodorus, there were Critobulus and his father Crito, Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, and Antisthenes. Also Ctesippus from the deme of Paeania, Menexenus, and a few others. Plato, if I remember correctly, was ill.
ECHECRATES: Were there any strangers?
PHAEDO: Yes, there were — Simmias the Theban, Cebes, and Phaedondes; and Euclid and Terpsion, who came from Megara.
ECHECRATES: And was Aristippus there, and Cleombrotus?
PHAEDO: No, they were said to be in Aegina.
ECHECRATES: Anyone else?
PHAEDO: I think that was just about everyone.
ECHECRATES: Well, then — what did you talk about?

PHAEDO: I'll start at the beginning and try to repeat the whole conversation. On the previous days, we had been in the habit of gathering early in the morning at the court where the trial had taken place, not far from the prison. There we would wait and talk together until the doors were opened — they weren't opened early — and then we would go in and usually spend the day with Socrates. On this last morning, we gathered earlier than usual, because the evening before, when we left the prison, we had heard that the sacred ship had returned from Delos. So we arranged to meet very early at our usual spot. When we arrived, the jailer who answered the door, instead of letting us in, came out and told us to wait until he called us. 'The Eleven,' he said, 'are with Socrates now. They're taking off his chains and giving orders that he is to die today.' Soon he returned and said we could go in. On entering, we found Socrates just released from his chains. Xanthippe — whom you know — was sitting beside him, holding their child in her arms. When she saw us, she cried out and said the kind of thing women say: 'Socrates, this is the last time either you will talk with your friends, or they with you.' Socrates turned to Crito and said: 'Crito, let someone take her home.' And some of Crito's people led her away, crying out and beating her breast.

When she was gone, Socrates sat up on the couch, bent his leg, and began to rub it, saying as he rubbed: How strange a thing is this which people call pleasure — and how curiously related to what seems to be its opposite, pain. The two are never present to a man at the same moment, and yet anyone who pursues one is generally forced to take the other as well. Their bodies are two, but they're joined by a single head. I can't help thinking that if Aesop had considered them, he would have made a fable about God trying to reconcile their quarrel — and finding he couldn't, so fastening their heads together. That would explain why, whenever one of them comes, the other follows close behind. I know this from my own experience right now, since after the pain in my leg from the chain, pleasure seems to follow.

At this, Cebes said: I'm glad, Socrates, that you've mentioned Aesop. It reminds me of a question that many people have been asking — Evenus the poet put it to me only the day before yesterday, and he'll be sure to ask it again. So if you want me to have an answer ready for him, tell me what I should say. He wanted to know why you, who never wrote a line of poetry before, now that you're in prison are turning Aesop's fables into verse and also composing that hymn in honor of Apollo.

Tell him the truth, Cebes, he said — that I had no thought of rivaling him or his poems. I knew that would be no easy task. I just wanted to see whether I could clear up a scruple I felt about the meaning of certain dreams. Throughout my life I've often had messages in dreams telling me 'to make music.' The same dream came to me sometimes in one form, sometimes in another, but always saying the same thing — or nearly so: 'Cultivate and make music,' the dream said. Up to now I had assumed this was only meant to urge and encourage me in the study of philosophy, which has been the pursuit of my life and which I took to be the noblest and best kind of music. The dream, I thought, was simply telling me to do what I was already doing — the way spectators shout at a runner to run when he's already running. But I wasn't certain of this. The dream might have meant music in the popular sense of the word. And since I'm under sentence of death, and the festival has given me this respite, I thought it would be safer to satisfy the scruple and — in obedience to the dream — compose a few verses before I depart.

So first I made a hymn in honor of the god whose festival it was. Then I reflected that a poet, if he is really to be a poet, should not merely put words together, but invent stories as well — and since I have no gift for invention, I took some fables of Aesop that I knew and had at hand (they were the first ones that came to mind) and turned them into verse. Tell this to Evenus, Cebes, and tell him to take heart. Tell him I'd have him follow me, if he's a wise man, and not linger behind — for today, apparently, I'm going. The Athenians say I must.
Simmias said: What a message for such a man! From what I know of Evenus — and I've spent a good deal of time with him — he'll never take your advice unless he's forced to.
Why? said Socrates. Isn't Evenus a philosopher?
I think he is, said Simmias.
Then he, and any man with the spirit of philosophy, will be willing to die. Though he will not take his own life — that is held to be unlawful.
Here he shifted his position, put his feet on the ground, and remained sitting like that for the rest of the conversation.
Then Cebes asked: Why do you say, Socrates, that a man ought not to take his own life, and yet that the philosopher will be ready to follow the dying?
Socrates replied: But Cebes and Simmias, you've both been students of Philolaus — have you never heard him speak about this?
Yes, but his language was obscure, Socrates.

My words are only an echo of what I've heard. But there's no reason I shouldn't repeat them. And indeed, since I'm going to another place, it's very fitting that I should be thinking and talking about the nature of the journey I'm about to make. What better way could I spend the time between now and sunset?

Then tell me, Socrates, why is suicide held to be unlawful? I have certainly heard Philolaus — the man you were just asking about — affirm it when he was staying with us at Thebes. And others say the same thing, though I've never understood what any of them meant by it.

Don't lose heart, Socrates replied; the day may come when you'll understand. I suppose you wonder why, when other things that seem evil can nevertheless be good at certain times and for certain people, death alone is to be the exception — why, when a man is better off dead, he is not allowed to do himself this favor, but must wait for the hand of another.
Very true, said Cebes, laughing gently and speaking in his Boeotian dialect.

I admit the appearance of inconsistency in what I'm saying — but there may be no real inconsistency in it after all. There is a doctrine whispered in secret that man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away. This is a great mystery which I don't entirely understand. And yet I too believe that the gods are our guardians, and that we are a possession of theirs. Don't you agree?
Yes, I quite agree, said Cebes.

And if one of your own possessions — an ox or an ass, for instance — took it upon itself to put itself out of the way, without your having given any sign that you wished it to die, wouldn't you be angry with it? And wouldn't you punish it if you could?
Certainly, replied Cebes.
Then looked at in this way, there's reason in saying that a man should wait, and not take his own life, until God summons him — as he is now summoning me.

Yes, Socrates, said Cebes, there seems to be truth in what you say. And yet, how can you reconcile this seemingly true belief — that God is our guardian and we are his possession — with the willingness to die that we were just attributing to the philosopher? It doesn't seem reasonable that the wisest of men should be willing to leave a service in which they are ruled by gods who are the best of masters. Surely no wise man thinks that once set at liberty, he can take better care of himself than the gods take of him. A fool might think so — he might argue that he had better run away from his master, without considering that his duty is to remain to the end, not to run away from what is good, and that there would be no sense in running. The wise man, on the other hand, will want to stay forever with whoever is better than himself. Now this, Socrates, is the reverse of what was just said. On this view, the wise man should grieve at leaving life, and the fool should rejoice.
Cebes's earnestness seemed to please Socrates. Here, he said, turning to us, is a man who is always asking questions, and is not so easily satisfied by the first thing he hears.

And certainly, Simmias added, the objection Cebes is now making seems to me to have some force. What could it mean for a truly wise man to want to fly away and lightly leave a master who is better than himself? I rather think Cebes is referring to you — he thinks you're too ready to leave us, and too ready to leave the gods whom you yourself acknowledge to be our good masters.
Yes, Socrates replied, there is reason in what you say. So you think I ought to answer the indictment, as if I were still in court?
We'd like you to, said Simmias.

Then I must try to make a more successful defense before you than I did before the judges. For I'll readily admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I ought to be grieved at death — if I weren't persuaded, first, that I'm going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be about any such thing), and second (though I'm less sure about this) that I'm going to people who have departed, who are better than those I leave behind. That's why I don't grieve as I might have done — because I have good hope that there is still something left for the dead, and, as has been said of old, some far better thing for the good than for the evil.

But do you mean to take your thoughts away with you, Socrates? said Simmias. Won't you share them with us? They're a benefit that we too are entitled to share. Besides, if you succeed in convincing us, that will be your answer to the charge against yourself.
I'll do my best, Socrates replied. But first let me hear what Crito wants — he has long been wishing to say something to me.

Only this, Socrates, replied Crito. The attendant who is to give you the poison has been telling me — and he wants me to tell you — that you are not to talk much. Talking, he says, increases heat, and heat interferes with the action of the poison. People who get themselves worked up sometimes have to take a second or even a third dose.
Then, said Socrates, let him mind his own business and be prepared to give the poison twice, or even three times, if necessary. That's all.
I knew quite well what you'd say, Crito replied, but I had to satisfy him.
Never mind him, Socrates said.

And now, my judges, I want to prove to you that the real philosopher has reason to be cheerful when he is about to die, and that after death he may hope to attain the greatest good in the other world. And how this can be, Simmias and Cebes, I'll try to explain. For I think that the true devotee of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by other men. They don't see that he is always pursuing death and dying — and if this is so, and he has had the desire of death all his life long, why on earth, when his time finally comes, should he complain about the very thing he has always been pursuing and desiring?

Simmias laughed and said: Though I'm not in a laughing mood, Socrates, you've made me laugh. I can't help thinking that the many, when they hear this, will say how truly you have described philosophers — and our own people back home will likewise say that the life which philosophers desire is really death, and that they've at last been found out to deserve the very death they desire.

chapters.title: The Philosopher and Death
paragraphs: And they are right, Simmias, in thinking that — with the exception of the words 'they have been found out.' Because they have not found out what the nature of this death is that the true philosopher deserves, or in what sense he deserves or desires it. But let's leave them aside and discuss the matter among ourselves. Do we believe there is such a thing as death?
To be sure, Simmias replied.

Isn't it the separation of soul and body? And to be dead is the completion of this — when the soul exists in herself and is released from the body, and the body is released from the soul. What is this but death?
Just so, he replied.

There's another question, which may throw light on our present inquiry, if you and I can agree about it: Ought the philosopher to care about the pleasures — if we can call them pleasures — of eating and drinking?
Certainly not, answered Simmias.
And what about the pleasures of love — should he care for them?
By no means.

And would he think much of the other ways of indulging the body — acquiring costly clothes, or fine sandals, or other adornments? Rather than caring about them, doesn't he despise anything beyond what nature needs? What do you say?
I would say that the true philosopher despises them.
Wouldn't you say that he is entirely concerned with the soul and not with the body? He would like, so far as he can, to get away from the body and turn toward the soul.
Quite true.
In these matters, above all other men, philosophers may be observed in every sort of way to separate the soul from the communion of the body.
Very true.

Whereas, Simmias, the rest of the world thinks that to someone who has no sense of pleasure and no share in bodily pleasure, life is not worth having — and that the man who is indifferent to such things is as good as dead.
That is also true.

And what shall we say about the actual acquisition of knowledge? Is the body, if invited to share in the inquiry, a help or a hindrance? I mean: do sight and hearing have any truth in them? Aren't they, as the poets are always telling us, inaccurate witnesses? And if even they are inaccurate and unclear, what shall we say about the other senses? — for you'll grant that they are the best of them.
Certainly, he replied.
Then when does the soul attain truth? In trying to consider anything together with the body, she is obviously deceived.
True.
So must not true existence be revealed to her in thought, if at all?
Yes.

And thought is best when the mind is gathered into herself and none of these things trouble her — neither sounds nor sights nor pain nor any pleasure — when she takes leave of the body, has as little as possible to do with it, has no bodily sense or desire, and aspires only after true being.
Certainly.
And in this the philosopher dishonors the body — his soul runs away from his body and desires to be alone by herself?
That is true.
Well, but here's another point, Simmias: Is there, or is there not, an absolute justice?
Assuredly there is.
And an absolute beauty, and an absolute good?
Of course.
But did you ever behold any of them with your eyes?
Certainly not.

Or did you ever reach them with any other bodily sense? I'm speaking not only of these, but of absolute greatness, and health, and strength — and of the essence or true nature of everything. Has the reality of such things ever been perceived by you through the bodily organs? Isn't it rather that the nearest approach to the knowledge of each of them is made by someone who so orders his intellectual vision as to have the most exact conception of the essence of whatever he is considering?
Certainly.

And he attains the purest knowledge of them who goes to each with the mind alone — not introducing or intruding into the act of thought sight or any other sense together with reason, but with the very light of the mind in her own clearness searching for the truth of each thing. He who has got rid, as far as he can, of eyes and ears, and — so to speak — of the whole body, since these are in his view distracting elements which, when they infect the soul, hinder her from acquiring truth and knowledge — he, and no one else, is likely to attain the knowledge of true being.
What you say has a wonderful truth in it, Socrates, replied Simmias.

And when real philosophers consider all this, won't they be led to a reflection, which they would express in words something like these? 'Haven't we found,' they will say, 'a path of thought which seems to bring us and our argument to this conclusion: that while we are in the body, and while the soul is infected with the evils of the body, our desire will not be satisfied? And our desire is for the truth. The body is a source of endless trouble for us, simply from the requirement of being fed; and it is also liable to diseases which overtake us and hinder us in the search for true being. It fills us with loves and lusts and fears, with fancies of every kind and endless foolery, and — as people rightly say — takes away from us the power of thinking at all. Where do wars and quarrels and factions come from? From the body and the lusts of the body. Wars are caused by the love of money, and money must be acquired for the sake and in the service of the body. And because of all these impediments, we have no time to spare for philosophy. Worst of all, even when we do have leisure and turn to some inquiry, the body is constantly interrupting us, causing turmoil and confusion, and dazzling us so that we cannot see the truth.

Experience has shown us that if we want to have pure knowledge of anything, we must be free of the body — the soul in herself must behold things in themselves. Then, and only then, we will attain the wisdom we desire — and of which we say we are lovers — not while we live, but after death. Because if, while in the company of the body, the soul cannot have pure knowledge, then one of two things follows: either knowledge is not to be attained at all, or, if at all, only after death. For then, and not until then, the soul will be separated from the body and exist in herself alone. In this present life, I think we make the nearest approach to knowledge when we have the least possible intercourse or communion with the body, are not surfeited by bodily nature, and keep ourselves pure until the hour when God himself is pleased to release us. And thus, having rid ourselves of the foolishness of the body, we shall be pure and hold converse with the pure, and know of ourselves the clear light that is everywhere — which is nothing else but the light of truth.' For the impure are not permitted to approach the pure. These are the sort of words, Simmias, that the true lovers of knowledge cannot help saying to one another and thinking. You'd agree, wouldn't you?
Undoubtedly, Socrates.

But, my friend, if this is true, there is great reason to hope that when I arrive where I am going — at the end of my journey — I shall attain what has been the pursuit of my life. And so I go on my way rejoicing, and not I only, but every other man who believes that his mind has been made ready and is, in a way, purified.
Certainly, Simmias replied.

And what is purification, if not the separation of the soul from the body, as I was saying before? The habit of the soul gathering and collecting herself into herself out of the body on all sides — dwelling in her own place alone, as in another life, so also in this, as far as she can — the release of the soul from the chains of the body?
Very true, he said.
And this separation and release of the soul from the body is what we call death?
To be sure, he said.
And the true philosophers, and they alone, are always seeking to release the soul. Isn't this separation and release of the soul from the body precisely their study?
That is true.
Then, as I was saying at first, it would be a ridiculous contradiction for men to study to live as closely as possible to a state of death, and then complain when death actually comes upon them.
Clearly.

And the true philosophers, Simmias, are always practicing death — which is why death is least terrible of all to them. Look at it this way: if they have been in every way the enemies of the body, and are longing to be alone with the soul, how absurd it would be when their desire is granted for them to tremble and complain, instead of rejoicing at their departure to that place where, when they arrive, they hope to gain what they desired in life — which was wisdom — and at the same time be rid of the company of their enemy. Many a man has been willing to go to the world below in hope of seeing there an earthly love, or a wife, or a son, and of conversing with them. And will someone who is a true lover of wisdom, and is firmly convinced that only in the world below can he enjoy her to the full — will he still complain at death? Won't he depart with joy? He surely will, my friend, if he is a true philosopher. He will have a firm conviction that there, and only there, he can find wisdom in her purity. And if this is true, he would be utterly absurd, as I said, if he were afraid of death.
He would, indeed, replied Simmias.

And when you see a man complaining as death approaches, isn't his reluctance sufficient proof that he is not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body — and probably, at the same time, a lover of either money or power, or both?
Quite so, he replied.
And isn't courage, Simmias, a quality specially characteristic of the philosopher?
Certainly.

And temperance, which even the common people understand as control and regulation of the passions, and a sense of superiority to them — isn't temperance a virtue belonging only to those who despise the body and spend their lives in philosophy?
Most assuredly.
For the courage and temperance of other men, if you look at them closely, are really a contradiction.
How so?
Well, he said, you know that death is regarded by people in general as a great evil.
Very true, he said.
And don't courageous men face death because they are afraid of even greater evils?
That is quite true.
Then all except philosophers are courageous only from fear, and because they are afraid. And yet that a man should be courageous out of fear, and out of cowardice, is surely strange.
Very true.

And aren't the temperate people in exactly the same case? They are temperate because they are intemperate — which might seem a contradiction, yet it's the sort of thing that happens with this foolish temperance. There are pleasures they are afraid of losing, and in their desire to keep them, they abstain from some pleasures because they are overcome by others. Although being conquered by pleasure is what men call intemperance, to them the conquest of pleasure consists in being conquered by pleasure. That is what I mean by saying that, in a sense, they are made temperate through intemperance.
Such appears to be the case.

Yet the exchange of one fear or pleasure or pain for another fear or pleasure or pain — the greater for the less, as if they were coins — is not the exchange of virtue. My blessed Simmias, is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged? And that coin is wisdom. Only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold — whether courage, or temperance, or justice. Isn't all true virtue the companion of wisdom, no matter what fears or pleasures or similar goods or evils may or may not attend her? But the virtue that is made up of these goods, severed from wisdom and exchanged with one another, is only a shadow of virtue; there's no freedom or health or truth in her. The true exchange is a purging away of all these things, and temperance, and justice, and courage, and wisdom herself are this very purgation. The founders of the mysteries must have had a real meaning — they were not talking nonsense — when they hinted long ago in a figure that he who passes unsanctified and uninitiated into the world below will lie in a mire, but that he who arrives there after initiation and purification will dwell with the gods.

For 'many,' as they say in the mysteries, 'are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics' — meaning, as I interpret it, 'the true philosophers.' To be counted among their number is what I have been seeking, according to my ability, all my life. Whether I have sought in the right way or not, and whether I have succeeded, I shall truly know in a little while, if God wills, when I myself arrive in the other world. That is my belief. And therefore I maintain, Simmias and Cebes, that I am right in not grieving or complaining at being parted from you and from my masters in this world, because I believe that I shall equally find good masters and friends in another world. But most men do not believe this. If, then, I succeed in convincing you by my defense better than I did the Athenian judges, it will be well.

Cebes answered: I agree, Socrates, with the greater part of what you say. But when it comes to the soul, men tend to be skeptical. They fear that when she has left the body, her place may be nowhere, and that on the very day of death she may perish and come to an end — dispersing like smoke or air as soon as she is released from the body, and in her flight vanishing into nothingness. If she could only be collected into herself after she has been released from the evils you speak of, there would be good reason to hope, Socrates, that what you say is true. But surely it takes a great deal of argument and many proofs to show that when a man is dead, his soul still exists, and still has any force or intelligence.
True, Cebes, said Socrates. Then shall I suggest that we discuss the likelihood of these things a little?
I am sure, said Cebes, that I would very much like to know your opinion about them.

I reckon, said Socrates, that no one who heard me now — not even one of my old enemies, the Comic poets — could accuse me of idle talking about matters that don't concern me. If you're agreeable, then, let's proceed with the inquiry.

chapters.title: The Argument from Opposites
paragraphs: Suppose we consider the question of whether the souls of men after death are, or are not, in the world below. There's an ancient doctrine which comes to mind — that they go from here into the other world, and returning again, are born from the dead. If it's true that the living come from the dead, then our souls must exist in that other world — for otherwise, how could they have been born again? This would be conclusive if there were any real evidence that the living are only born from the dead; but if that isn't so, then other arguments will have to be brought in.
Very true, replied Cebes.

Then let's consider the whole question — not in relation to human beings only, but in relation to animals generally, and to plants, and to everything that has generation. The proof will be easier that way. Are not all things which have opposites generated from their opposites? I mean such things as good and evil, just and unjust — and there are countless other opposites generated from opposites. I want to show that in all opposites there must be a similar alternation. For example: anything which becomes greater must become greater after having been less.
True.
And that which becomes less must have been greater before, and then have become less.
Yes.
And the weaker is generated from the stronger, and the swifter from the slower.
Very true.
And the worse is from the better, and the more just from the more unjust.
Of course.
And is this true of all opposites? Are we convinced that all of them are generated from opposites?
Yes.

And in this universal opposition of all things, aren't there always two intermediate processes going on — from one opposite to the other, and back again? Where there's a greater and a less, there's also an intermediate process of increase and diminution — what grows is said to wax, and what decays to wane.
Yes, he said.

And there are many other processes, such as division and composition, cooling and heating, which likewise involve a passage into and out of one another. This necessarily holds of all opposites, even though it isn't always expressed in words — they really are generated out of one another, and there is a passing or process from one to the other of them.
Very true, he replied.
Well — isn't there an opposite of life, just as sleep is the opposite of waking?
True, he said.
And what is it?
Death, he answered.
And these, if they are opposites, are generated one from the other, and have their two intermediate processes as well?
Of course.

Now, said Socrates, I'll analyze one of the two pairs of opposites I've mentioned, along with its intermediate processes, and you shall analyze the other for me. One pair I'll call sleep, the other waking. The state of sleep is opposed to the state of waking; out of sleeping, waking is generated, and out of waking, sleeping. The process of generation is, in the one case, falling asleep, and in the other, waking up. Do you agree?
I entirely agree.
Then you analyze life and death for me in the same way. Isn't death opposed to life?
Yes.
And they are generated from one another?
Yes.
What is generated from the living?
The dead.
And what is generated from the dead?
I can only say — the living.
Then the living, Cebes — whether things or persons — are generated from the dead?
That is clear, he replied.
Then the inference is that our souls exist in the world below?
That is true.
And one of the two processes or generations is visible — for surely the act of dying is visible?
Surely, he said.
What, then, is to be the result? Shall we exclude the opposite process? And suppose nature walks on one leg only? Mustn't we rather assign to death some corresponding process of generation?
Certainly, he replied.
And what is that process?
Return to life.
And return to life, if there is such a thing, is the birth of the dead into the world of the living?
Quite true.

Then here is a new way by which we arrive at the conclusion that the living come from the dead, just as the dead come from the living. And this, if true, affords a most certain proof that the souls of the dead exist in some place out of which they come again.
Yes, Socrates, he said — the conclusion seems to flow necessarily from our previous admissions.

And that these admissions were not unfair, Cebes, can, I think, be shown this way. If generation were in a straight line only, with no compensation or circle in nature — no turn or return of elements into their opposites — then you know that all things would at last have the same form, pass into the same state, and there would be no more generation.
What do you mean? he said.

A simple enough thing, which I'll illustrate by the case of sleep, he replied. You know that if there were no alternation of sleeping and waking, the tale of Endymion sleeping forever would in the end have no meaning, because all other things would be asleep too, and he wouldn't be distinguishable from the rest. Or if there were composition only, and no division of substances, then the chaos of Anaxagoras would come again. In the same way, my dear Cebes, if all things that partook of life were to die, and after they were dead remained in the form of death, and didn't come to life again, then all would eventually die, and nothing would be alive. What other result could there be? If the living spring from some other thing, and they too die, mustn't all things at last be swallowed up in death? (Compare Republic.)
There's no escape, Socrates, said Cebes — and to me your argument seems absolutely true.

Yes, he said, Cebes, it is and must be so, in my opinion. We haven't been deluded in making these admissions. I am confident that there truly is such a thing as living again, that the living spring from the dead, that the souls of the dead are in existence, and that the good souls have a better portion than the evil.

chapters.title: The Argument from Recollection
paragraphs: Cebes added: Your favorite doctrine, Socrates — that knowledge is simply recollection — if true, also necessarily implies a previous time in which we learned what we now recollect. But this would be impossible unless our soul had been somewhere before existing in human form. Here, then, is another proof of the soul's immortality.
But tell me, Cebes, Simmias broke in, what are the arguments in favor of this doctrine of recollection? I'm not quite sure I remember them at the moment.

One excellent proof, said Cebes, comes from questioning. If you ask someone a question the right way, he will give a true answer on his own — but how could he do this unless there were knowledge and right reason already in him? This is most clearly shown when he's taken to a diagram or something of that sort. (Compare Meno.)

But if you're still unconvinced, Simmias, said Socrates, let me ask whether you may not agree with me when the matter is looked at another way — I mean, if you still doubt whether knowledge is recollection.

It's not that I'm unconvinced, said Simmias; but I want this very doctrine of recollection brought back to my own recollection. From what Cebes has said I'm beginning to remember, and I'm being convinced — but I'd still like to hear what you were going to say.
This is what I'd say, he replied: We would agree, if I'm not mistaken, that whatever a man recollects he must have known at some earlier time.
Very true.

And what is the nature of this knowledge, or of recollection? I mean: when a person, having seen or heard or in any way perceived something, knows not only that thing but also forms a conception of something else — a thing that is the object of a different kind of knowledge — may he not fairly be said to recollect that of which he has formed the conception?
What do you mean?
Let me illustrate by an example. The knowledge of a lyre is not the same as the knowledge of a man.
True.

And yet you know the feeling of lovers when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else the beloved has been in the habit of using. From knowing the lyre, they form in their mind's eye the image of the young man the lyre belongs to. That is recollection. In the same way, anyone who sees Simmias may remember Cebes — and there are endless examples of the same thing.
Endless, indeed, replied Simmias.
And recollection is most commonly the recovering of something that has been forgotten through time and inattention.
Very true, he said.
Well — and may you not also, from seeing the picture of a horse or a lyre, remember a man? And from the picture of Simmias, may you not be led to remember Cebes?
True.
Or you might also be led to the recollection of Simmias himself?
Quite so.
And in all these cases, the recollection may be derived from things either like or unlike the thing recollected?
It may be.
And when the recollection is derived from like things, another consideration is sure to arise — namely, whether the likeness in any degree falls short of that which is recollected.
Very true, he said.

chapters.title: The Affinity Argument
paragraphs: And shall we go one step further and affirm that there is such a thing as equality itself—not the equality of one piece of wood or stone with another, but over and above those, an absolute equality? Shall we say so?
Say so, yes, Simmias replied, and swear to it with all the confidence in the world.
And do we know the nature of this absolute essence?
To be sure, he said.

And where did we get that knowledge? Didn't we see equalities in material things—pieces of wood and stones and the like—and from those gather the idea of an equality that is different from them? You'll grant there's a difference. Or look at it another way: don't the very same pieces of wood or stone appear equal at one time and unequal at another?
That's certainly true.
But are things that are truly equal ever unequal? Or is the idea of equality the same as that of inequality?
Impossible, Socrates.
Then these so-called equals are not the same as the idea of equality itself?
Clearly not, Socrates.
And yet from these equals, different as they are from the idea of equality, you conceived that idea and reached it?
Very true, he said.
An idea which might be either like them or unlike them?
Yes.
But that makes no difference. Whenever from seeing one thing you conceive another—whether like or unlike—there must surely have been an act of recollection?
Very true.

Now what would you say about equal pieces of wood and stone, or other material equals? What impression do they make? Are they equal in the same sense in which absolute equality is equal? Or do they fall short of that perfect equality in some measure?
Yes, he said, and by a very great measure too.

And must we not grant this: when someone looks at an object and notices that it aims at being another thing, but falls short of it and cannot be that other thing, but is inferior to it—whoever makes this observation must have had previous knowledge of that thing to which the other, though similar, was inferior?
Certainly.
And hasn't this been our own case with equals and absolute equality?
Precisely.
Then we must have known equality before the time when we first saw material equals and reflected that all these apparent equals strive to reach absolute equality but fall short of it?
Very true.
And we also recognize that this absolute equality is known, and can only be known, through sight or touch or some other of the senses, which are all alike in this respect?
Yes, Socrates, as far as the argument is concerned, one sense is as good as another.
So it is from the senses that we derive the knowledge that all sensible things aim at an absolute equality which they fall short of?
Yes.

Then before we began to see or hear or perceive in any way, we must have had knowledge of absolute equality—otherwise we could not have referred to that standard the equals derived from the senses. For to that they all aspire, and of that they all fall short.
No other conclusion can be drawn from what was said before.
And did we not see and hear and make use of our other senses as soon as we were born?
Certainly.
Then we must have acquired the knowledge of equality at some earlier time?
Yes.
That is to say, before we were born, I suppose?
True.

And if we acquired this knowledge before we were born, and were born already possessing it, then we knew before birth and at the very moment of birth not only the equal or the greater or the less, but all other Ideas as well. For we are not speaking only of equality, but of beauty, goodness, justice, holiness, and everything we mark with the name of essence in the dialectical process, both when we ask and when we answer questions. Of all this we can certainly affirm that we acquired the knowledge before birth?
We can.

But if, after acquiring it, we have not forgotten what we learned in each case, then we must always have come into life already knowing, and must always continue to know as long as life lasts—for knowing is acquiring and retaining knowledge and not forgetting. Isn't forgetting, Simmias, just the losing of knowledge?
Quite true, Socrates.

But if the knowledge we acquired before birth was lost by us at birth, and if afterwards, by use of the senses, we recovered what we previously knew, then won't the process we call learning be a recovering of knowledge that is natural to us—and mightn't this rightly be called recollection?
Very true.

So much is clear: when we perceive something by sight, hearing, or another sense, from that perception we can get a notion of some other thing, like or unlike, which is associated with it but has been forgotten. So, as I was saying, one of two alternatives follows: either we had this knowledge at birth and continued to know throughout life; or else those said to learn, after birth, are only remembering, and learning is simply recollection.
Yes, that is quite true, Socrates.
And which alternative, Simmias, do you prefer? Did we have the knowledge at birth, or do we recollect the things we knew prior to birth?
I cannot decide at the moment.
At any rate you can decide this: will someone who has knowledge be able to give an account of it, or not? What do you say?
Certainly, he will.
But do you think every man is able to give an account of the matters we are discussing?
I wish they could, Socrates, but I rather fear that tomorrow, at this time, there will no longer be anyone alive able to give such an account as ought to be given.
Then you are not of the opinion, Simmias, that all men know these things?
Certainly not.
They are in the process of recollecting what they learned before?
Certainly.
But when did our souls acquire this knowledge?—not since we were born as men?
Certainly not.
And therefore, at some earlier time?
Yes.
Then, Simmias, our souls must also have existed without bodies before they took human form, and must have had intelligence.
Unless, Socrates, you suppose these notions are given to us at the very moment of birth—for that is the only time that remains.
Yes, my friend, but if so, when do we lose them? We agreed they are not in us when we are born. Do we lose them at the moment of receiving them, or if not then, at what other time?
No, Socrates—I see that I was unconsciously talking nonsense.

Then may we not say this, Simmias: if, as we keep repeating, there is an absolute beauty, and goodness, and an absolute essence of all things; and if we refer all our sensations to this essence—which now proves to have existed in our former state—and compare them with it, finding these Ideas to be pre-existent and our inborn possession—then our souls must have had a prior existence; but if not, there would be no force in the argument? The proof that these Ideas must have existed before we were born is the same as the proof that our souls existed before we were born; and if not the Ideas, then not the souls.

Yes, Socrates; I am convinced that there is exactly the same necessity for the one as for the other, and the argument retreats safely to the position that the existence of the soul before birth cannot be separated from the existence of the essence you speak of. For to my mind nothing is more evident than that beauty, goodness, and the other notions you were just now mentioning have a most real and absolute existence; and I am satisfied with the proof.
Well, but is Cebes equally satisfied? For I must convince him too.

I think, Simmias said, that Cebes is satisfied—although he is the most incredulous of mortals, I believe he is sufficiently convinced of the existence of the soul before birth. But that the soul will continue to exist after death is not yet proven even to my own satisfaction. I cannot shake the feeling of the many to which Cebes was referring—the feeling that when a man dies the soul may be dispersed, and that this may be the end of her. For granted that she may have been born elsewhere, framed out of other elements, and was in existence before entering the human body, why, after she has entered in and then gone out again, may she not herself be destroyed and come to an end?

Very true, Simmias, said Cebes; about half of what is required has been proven—namely, that our souls existed before we were born. That the soul will exist after death as well as before birth is the other half, still needing proof; when that is given, the demonstration will be complete.

But that proof, Simmias and Cebes, has already been given, said Socrates, if you put the two arguments together—I mean this one and the earlier one, in which we admitted that everything living is born from the dead. For if the soul exists before birth, and in coming to life and being born can only be born from death and dying, must she not also continue to exist after death, since she has to be born again?—Surely the proof you want has already been supplied. Still, I suspect that you and Simmias would be glad to press the argument further. Like children, you are haunted by the fear that when the soul leaves the body the wind may really blow her away and scatter her—especially if a man happens to die in a great storm and not when the sky is calm.

Cebes answered with a smile: Then, Socrates, you must argue us out of our fears—though strictly speaking they are not our fears, but there is a child within us to whom death is a kind of hobgoblin; him too we must persuade not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark.
Socrates said: Let the voice of the charmer be applied daily until you have charmed the fear away.
And where shall we find a good charmer of our fears, Socrates, when you are gone?

Hellas, he replied, is a large place, Cebes, and has many good men, and there are no few barbarian peoples either: seek such a charmer among them all, far and wide, sparing neither effort nor money; for there is no better way to spend your money. And you must search among yourselves too, for you will not find others more able to make the search.
The search, replied Cebes, shall certainly be made. And now, if you please, let us return to the point in the argument at which we digressed.
By all means, replied Socrates; what else should I please?
Very good.

Must we not ask ourselves, said Socrates, what sort of thing it is that we imagine to be liable to be scattered, and about which we fear? And what sort of thing it is about which we have no fear? And then we can go on to inquire whether that which suffers dispersion is of the nature of soul or not—our hopes and fears about our own souls will turn on the answers to these questions.
Very true, he said.

Now the compound or composite may be supposed naturally capable of being dissolved, just as it was of being compounded; but the uncompounded—and only the uncompounded—must be, if anything is, indissoluble.
Yes; I should imagine so, said Cebes.
And the uncompounded may be assumed to be the same and unchanging, whereas the compound is always changing and never the same.
I agree, he said.

Then let us return to the earlier discussion. That Idea or essence which in the dialectical process we define as essence or true existence—whether the essence of equality, of beauty, or of anything else—are these essences ever liable to some degree of change? Or is each of them always what it is, having the same simple self-existent and unchanging form, admitting no variation at all, in any way, or at any time?
They must always be the same, Socrates, replied Cebes.

And what would you say of the many beautiful things—whether men or horses or garments or anything else called by the same names and spoken of as equal or beautiful? Are they all unchanging and always the same, or quite the reverse? Might they not rather be described as almost always changing and hardly ever the same, either with themselves or with one another?
The latter, replied Cebes; they are always in a state of change.
And these you can touch and see and perceive with the senses, but the unchanging things you can only perceive with the mind—they are invisible and are not seen?
That is very true, he said.
Well then, Socrates added, let us suppose there are two sorts of existences—one seen, the other unseen.
Let us suppose them.
The seen is the changing, and the unseen is the unchanging?
That may also be supposed.
And further, is not one part of us body, and another part soul?
To be sure.
And to which class is the body more alike and akin?
Clearly to the seen—no one can doubt that.
And is the soul seen, or not seen?
Not by man, Socrates.
And what we mean by 'seen' and 'not seen' is what is or is not visible to the eye of man?
Yes, to the eye of man.
And is the soul seen, or not seen?
Not seen.
Unseen, then?
Yes.
Then the soul is more like the unseen, and the body more like the seen?
That follows necessarily, Socrates.

And weren't we saying long ago that the soul, when using the body as an instrument of perception—that is, when using the sense of sight or hearing or some other sense (for perceiving through the body means perceiving through the senses)—weren't we saying that the soul is then dragged by the body into the region of the changeable, and wanders and is confused? The world spins round her, and she is like a drunkard whenever she touches change?
Very true.

But when she returns into herself and reflects, then she passes into the other world—the region of purity, eternity, immortality, and unchangeableness, which are her kindred; and with them she forever dwells whenever she is by herself and is not hindered. Then she ceases from her wandering, and being in communion with the unchanging, is herself unchanging. And this state of the soul is called wisdom?
That is well and truly said, Socrates, he replied.
And to which class is the soul more nearly alike and akin, as far as may be inferred from this argument and from the one before?
I think, Socrates, that in the opinion of anyone who follows the argument, the soul will be infinitely more like the unchangeable—even the most stupid person would not deny that.
And the body is more like the changing?
Yes.

Consider the matter once more in another light. When the soul and the body are united, nature orders the soul to rule and govern, and the body to obey and serve. Now which of these two functions is akin to the divine, and which to the mortal? Doesn't the divine appear to you to be that which naturally orders and rules, and the mortal to be that which is subject and servant?
True.
And which does the soul resemble?
The soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal—there can be no doubt of that, Socrates.

Then reflect, Cebes: of all that has been said, is this not the conclusion?—that the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal, and intellectual, and uniform, and indissoluble, and unchangeable; and that the body is in the very likeness of the human, and mortal, and unintellectual, and multiform, and dissoluble, and changeable. Can this, my dear Cebes, be denied?
It cannot.
But if so, then is not the body liable to speedy dissolution? And is not the soul almost or altogether indissoluble?
Certainly.

Observe further: after a man is dead, the body—the visible part of him, which lies in the visible world and is called a corpse, and would naturally be dissolved and decomposed and scattered—does not dissolve or decompose at once, but may remain for some time, even a long time, if the constitution was sound at the time of death and the season of the year is favorable. For the body, when shrunk and embalmed as they do in Egypt, may remain almost whole for countless ages; and even in decay, some parts such as the bones and ligaments are practically indestructible. Do you agree?
Yes.

And is it likely that the soul, which is invisible, in passing to the place of the true Hades—which, like her, is invisible, and pure, and noble, and on her way to the good and wise God (where, if God wills, my soul too is soon to go)—is it likely, I say, that the soul, if this be her nature and origin, will be blown away and destroyed the moment she leaves the body, as the many say? That can never be, my dear Simmias and Cebes. The truth rather is this: the soul which is pure at departing and drags no bodily taint after her, having never willingly during life had anything to do with the body—which she has always been avoiding, gathering herself into herself, and making such abstraction her constant practice—which means that she has been a true disciple of philosophy, and has therefore in fact always been practicing how to die. For is not philosophy the practice of death?—
Certainly—

That soul, I say, herself invisible, departs to the invisible world—to the divine, the immortal, the rational. On arriving there, she is secure of bliss and is released from the error and folly of men, from their fears and wild passions and all other human evils, and forever dwells, as they say of the initiated, in the company of the gods. Is this not true, Cebes?
Yes, said Cebes, beyond a doubt.

But the soul that has been polluted, and is impure at the time of her departure, and has been the companion and servant of the body always, and is in love with it and fascinated by it and by the body's desires and pleasures, until she comes to believe that the truth exists only in bodily form—something a man can touch and see and taste and use for his lusts—such a soul, accustomed to hate and fear and avoid the intellectual principle, which to the bodily eye is dark and invisible and can be attained only by philosophy—do you suppose that such a soul will depart pure and unalloyed?
Impossible, he replied.
She is held fast by the corporeal, which the continual association and constant care of the body have wrought into her nature.
Very true.

And this corporeal element, my friend, is heavy and weighty and earthy, and is that element of sight by which a soul is depressed and dragged down again into the visible world, because she is afraid of the invisible and of the world below—prowling about tombs and graves, near which, as they tell us, are seen certain ghostly apparitions of souls that have not departed pure, but are clogged with sight and therefore visible.
(Compare Milton, Comus:—

'But when lust, By unchaste looks, loose gestures, and foul talk, But most by lewd and lavish act of sin, Lets in defilement to the inward parts, The soul grows clotted by contagion, Imbodies, and imbrutes, till she quite lose, The divine property of her first being. Such are those thick and gloomy shadows damp Oft seen in charnel vaults and sepulchres, Lingering, and sitting by a new made grave, As loath to leave the body that it lov'd, And linked itself by carnal sensuality To a degenerate and degraded state.')
That is very likely, Socrates.

Yes, that is very likely, Cebes; and these must be the souls, not of the good, but of the wicked, which are compelled to wander about such places in payment of the penalty for their former evil way of life. And they continue to wander until, through the craving after the corporeal that never leaves them, they are at last imprisoned in another body. And they may be supposed to find their prisons in the same natures they had in their former lives.
What natures do you mean, Socrates?
I mean that men who have followed gluttony, wantonness, and drunkenness, and have never troubled to avoid them, would pass into asses and animals of that sort. What do you think?
I think that opinion to be exceedingly probable.
And those who have chosen the portion of injustice, tyranny, and violence will pass into wolves, or into hawks and kites—where else could we suppose them to go?
Yes, said Cebes; with such natures, beyond question.
And there is no difficulty, he said, in assigning to all of them places answering to their several natures and dispositions?
There is not, he said.

Some are happier than others; and the happiest, both in themselves and in the place they go, are those who have practiced the civil and social virtues called temperance and justice, which are acquired by habit and attention without philosophy and intelligence.
Why are they the happiest?

Because they may be expected to pass into some gentle and social kind which is like their own, such as bees or wasps or ants, or back again into the form of man; and just and moderate men may be supposed to spring from them.
Very likely.

No one who has not studied philosophy, and is not entirely pure at the time of his departure, is allowed to enter the company of the Gods—only the lover of knowledge is. And this is the reason, Simmias and Cebes, why the true devotees of philosophy abstain from all fleshly lusts, and hold out against them and refuse to give themselves up to them—not because they fear poverty or the ruin of their families, like the lovers of money and the world in general; nor like the lovers of power and honor, because they dread the dishonor and disgrace of evil deeds.
No, Socrates, that would not suit them, said Cebes.

No indeed, he replied; and therefore those who have any care of their own souls, and do not merely live molding and fashioning the body, say farewell to all this. They will not walk in the ways of the blind; and when philosophy offers them purification and release from evil, they feel they ought not to resist her influence, and wherever she leads they turn and follow.
What do you mean, Socrates?

I will tell you, he said. The lovers of knowledge are conscious that the soul was simply fastened and glued to the body—that until philosophy received her, she could view real existence only through the bars of a prison, not in and through herself; that she was wallowing in the mire of every kind of ignorance, and that through lust she had become the principal accomplice in her own captivity. This was her original state; and then, as I was saying, and as the lovers of knowledge are well aware, philosophy, seeing how dreadful her confinement was—of which she herself was the cause—received her and gently comforted her, and sought to release her, pointing out that the eye and the ear and the other senses are full of deception, and persuading her to withdraw from them, and to abstain from all but their necessary use, and to be gathered up and collected into herself, bidding her trust in herself and in her own pure apprehension of pure existence, and to mistrust whatever comes to her through other channels and is subject to variation; for such things are visible and tangible, but what she sees in her own nature is intelligible and invisible.

And the soul of the true philosopher thinks she ought not to resist this deliverance, and therefore abstains from pleasures and desires and pains and fears, as far as she is able—reflecting that when a man has great joys or sorrows or fears or desires, he suffers from them not merely the sort of evil one might expect, such as the loss of health or property that he has sacrificed to his lusts, but an evil far greater, the greatest and worst of all evils, and one that he never even thinks about.
What is it, Socrates? said Cebes.

The evil is this: when the feeling of pleasure or pain is most intense, every soul of man imagines that the objects of this intense feeling are then plainest and truest; but this is not so—they are really the things of sight.
Very true.
And is not this the state in which the soul is most enthralled by the body?
How so?

Why, because each pleasure and pain is a kind of nail that nails and rivets the soul to the body, until she becomes like the body and believes whatever the body affirms to be true. By agreeing with the body and sharing the same delights, she is forced to share the same habits and haunts, and is not likely ever to be pure at her departure to the world below, but is always infected by the body. And so she sinks into another body and germinates and grows there, and has therefore no share in the communion of the divine and pure and simple.
Most true, Socrates, answered Cebes.
And this, Cebes, is the reason why the true lovers of knowledge are temperate and brave; and not for the reason the world gives.
Certainly not.

Certainly not! The soul of a philosopher will reason in quite another way. She will not ask philosophy to release her so that when released she may deliver herself up again to the thraldom of pleasures and pains, doing a work only to undo it again, weaving instead of unweaving her Penelope's web. Rather, she will calm passion, and follow reason, and dwell in the contemplation of her, beholding the true and divine (which is no matter of opinion), and from that drawing her nourishment. Thus she seeks to live while she lives, and after death she hopes to go to her own kindred and to that which is like her, and to be freed from human ills. Never fear, Simmias and Cebes, that a soul which has been thus nurtured and has pursued these things will at her departure from the body be scattered and blown away by the winds and be nowhere and nothing.

When Socrates had finished speaking, there was silence for a considerable time. He himself seemed to be meditating, as most of us were, on what had been said; only Cebes and Simmias spoke a few words to one another. And Socrates, observing them, asked what they thought of the argument, and whether there was anything still wanting. For, said he, there are many points still open to suspicion and attack, if one were inclined to sift the matter thoroughly. If you are considering some other matter, I say no more; but if you are still in doubt, do not hesitate to say exactly what you think, and let us hear anything better you can suggest; and if you think I can be of any use, allow me to help you.

Simmias said: I must confess, Socrates, that doubts did arise in our minds, and each of us was urging and inciting the other to put the question we wanted answered, yet neither of us liked to ask, fearing that our importunity might be troublesome to you at such a time.

Socrates replied with a smile: O Simmias, what are you saying? I am hardly likely to persuade other men that I do not regard my present situation as a misfortune, if I cannot even persuade you that I am no worse off now than at any other time in my life. Will you not allow that I have as much of the spirit of prophecy in me as the swans? For when they perceive that they must die, having sung all their life long, they then sing more lustily than ever, rejoicing in the thought that they are about to depart to the god whose ministers they are. But men, because they are themselves afraid of death, slanderously say that the swans sing a lament at the last—not considering that no bird sings when cold or hungry or in pain, not even the nightingale, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, who are indeed said to tune a lay of sorrow, though I do not believe this to be true of them any more than of the swans. Rather, because they are sacred to Apollo, they have the gift of prophecy and foresee the good things of another world, which is why they sing and rejoice on that day more than they ever did before. And I too, believing myself to be the consecrated servant of the same God, and a fellow-servant of the swans, and thinking that I have received from my master gifts of prophecy not inferior to theirs, would not go out of life any less cheerfully than the swans.
Never mind that, then, if this is your only objection—but speak, and ask anything you like, while the eleven magistrates of Athens allow.

Very good, Socrates, said Simmias; then I will tell you my difficulty, and Cebes will tell you his. I feel myself (and I dare say you have the same feeling) how hard, or rather how impossible, it is to attain any certainty about questions such as these in the present life. And yet I should think him a coward who did not test what is said about them to the uttermost, or whose heart failed him before he had examined them on every side. He ought to persevere until he has achieved one of two things: either he should discover, or be taught, the truth about them; or, if that is impossible, he should take the best and most irrefragable of human theories, and let this be the raft upon which he sails through life—not without risk, as I admit, if he cannot find some word of God to carry him more surely and safely. And now, as you bid me, I will venture to question you, so that I shall not afterwards reproach myself with not having said at the time what I think. For when I consider the matter, either alone or with Cebes, the argument does certainly appear to me, Socrates, to be not sufficient.
Socrates answered: I dare say, my friend, that you may be right; but I should like to know in what respect the argument is insufficient.

chapters.title: The Objections
paragraphs: 'Here's my difficulty,' replied Simmias. 'Someone could use the same argument about a lyre and its harmony. They could say: harmony is invisible, incorporeal, perfectly beautiful, and divine — existing in a well-tuned lyre. But the lyre and its strings are material, composite, earthy, and mortal. Now if someone breaks the lyre or cuts the strings, your style of reasoning would lead us to say the harmony must survive — that surely the mortal lyre and broken strings still exist, so the harmony, being divine and immortal, can't have perished first. The harmony must still be somewhere, and the wood and strings will decay before anything happens to it. I imagine, Socrates, that you've had the same thought I have: that this is roughly our conception of the soul. When the body is strung together and held in balance by hot and cold, wet and dry, the soul is the harmony — the proper blending of these elements. If that's true, then whenever the body's strings are loosened or overstrained by disease or other injury, the soul — however divine — must immediately perish, just as other harmonies in music perish. The body's remains may last a long time before they're burned or decay. But the soul would be the first to be destroyed in what we call death.'
'And if someone insists that the soul, being a harmony of the body's elements, is the first to perish in death — how shall we answer him?'

Socrates looked intently at us with his penetrating eyes, smiled, and said: 'Simmias raises a fair point. If any of you has a better answer than I do, speak up — his attack has real force. But before we respond to him, I think we should hear what Cebes has to say as well, so we can take time to think. After hearing both, we can either agree with them if they're right, or defend our position if not. So tell me, Cebes — what was troubling you?'

chapters.title: The Final Argument
paragraphs: Cebes said: I'll tell you. My feeling is that the argument is where it was before, and open to the same objections that were urged earlier. I'm ready to admit that the existence of the soul before entering the bodily form has been very ingeniously — and, if I may say so, quite sufficiently — proven. But the existence of the soul after death is, in my judgment, still unproven. Now my objection is not the same as Simmias's. I'm not inclined to deny that the soul is stronger and more lasting than the body — my opinion is that the soul very far exceeds the body in all such respects. 'Well, then,' the argument says to me, 'why do you remain unconvinced? When you see that the weaker continues to exist after the man is dead, won't you admit that the more lasting must also survive during the same period of time?' Now let me ask you to consider whether the objection I'm going to raise — which, like Simmias, I'll express in a figure — carries any weight. The analogy I'll use is that of an old weaver who dies, and after his death someone says: 'He is not dead, he must still be alive — see, there is the coat he himself wove and wore, whole and undecayed.' And he goes on to ask someone who is skeptical whether a man lasts longer, or the coat in use and wear. When he's told that a man lasts far longer, he thinks he has conclusively demonstrated the survival of the man — who is the more lasting — because the less lasting still remains.

But that, Simmias, as I'd point out, is a mistake. Anyone can see that someone who talks that way is talking nonsense. The truth is that the weaver, having woven and worn many such coats, outlived several of them and was in turn outlived by the last one. But that doesn't prove that a man is slighter and weaker than a coat. The relation of the body to the soul may be expressed in a similar figure, and anyone may fairly say that the soul is lasting while the body is weak and short-lived in comparison. He may argue that every soul wears out many bodies — especially if a man lives many years. While he's alive, the body deliquesces and decays, and the soul is always weaving another garment and repairing the waste. But of course whenever the soul perishes, she must have her last garment on, and that will survive her. And then, when the soul is dead, the body will finally reveal its native weakness, and quickly decompose and pass away. So I'd rather not rely on the argument from superior strength to prove the continued existence of the soul after death.

For even granting more than you affirm to be possible — admitting not only that the soul existed before birth, but that the souls of some continue to exist after death, and are born and die again and again, and that there is a natural strength in the soul which holds out and is born many times — we may still be inclined to think that she will grow weary in the labors of successive births, and may at last succumb in one of her deaths and utterly perish. And this death and dissolution of the body which brings destruction to the soul may be unknown to any of us, because no one of us can have had experience of it. If that is so, then I maintain that whoever is confident about death has only a foolish confidence, unless he is able to prove that the soul is altogether immortal and imperishable. But if he can't prove the soul's immortality, anyone about to die will always have reason to fear that when the body is dissolved, the soul may utterly perish along with it.

All of us, as we afterwards admitted to one another, had an unpleasant feeling when we heard what they said. We had been so firmly convinced before, and now to have our faith shaken seemed to introduce confusion and uncertainty — not only into the previous argument, but into any future one. Either we were incapable of forming a judgment, or there were no grounds for belief at all.

ECHECRATES: There I feel with you — by heaven I do, Phaedo. While you were speaking, I was beginning to ask myself the same question: What argument can I ever trust again? What could be more convincing than the argument of Socrates, which has now fallen into discredit? That the soul is a harmony is a doctrine that has always had a wonderful appeal for me — and when you mentioned it, it came back to me at once as my own original conviction. And now I must begin again and find another argument to assure me that when the man is dead, the soul survives. Tell me, I beg you, how did Socrates proceed? Did he share the unpleasant feeling you mention? Or did he calmly meet the attack? And did he answer forcibly or feebly? Narrate what happened as exactly as you can.

PHAEDO: I have often wondered at Socrates, Echecrates, but never more than on that occasion. That he should be able to answer was nothing — what astonished me was, first, the gentle, pleasant, approving manner in which he received what the young men said, and then his quick sense of the wound the argument had inflicted, and the readiness with which he healed it. He might be compared to a general rallying his defeated and broken army, urging them to accompany him and return to the field of argument.
ECHECRATES: What followed?

PHAEDO: You shall hear. I was close to him on his right hand, seated on a sort of stool, while he was on a couch a good deal higher than me. He stroked my head and pressed the hair on my neck — he had a way of playing with my hair — and then he said: Tomorrow, Phaedo, I suppose these fair locks of yours will be cut off.
Yes, Socrates, I suppose they will, I replied.
Not so, if you'll take my advice.
What shall I do with them? I said.

Today, he replied, and not tomorrow, if this argument dies and we cannot bring it back to life again, you and I will both shave our hair. And if I were you, and the argument got away from me and I couldn't hold my ground against Simmias and Cebes, I would take an oath, like the Argives, not to wear my hair long again until I had renewed the battle and defeated them.
Yes, I said, but Heracles himself is said to be no match for two opponents.
Then summon me, he said, and I'll be your Iolaus until the sun goes down.
I summon you, then — though not as Heracles summoning Iolaus, but rather as Iolaus might summon Heracles.
That will do as well, he said. But first let's take care to avoid a danger.
Of what kind? I said.

Of becoming misologists, he replied. No worse thing can happen to a man than this. Just as there are misanthropists, or haters of men, there are also misologists — haters of ideas. Both spring from the same cause, which is ignorance of the world. Misanthropy arises out of the too-great confidence of inexperience. You trust a man and take him to be altogether true, sound, and faithful, and in a little while he turns out to be false and knavish. Then another, and another — and when this has happened several times, especially when it happens among those a man deems his most trusted and familiar friends, and he has often quarreled with them, he ends up hating everyone and believing that no one has any good in him at all. You must have observed this trait of character?
I have.

And isn't that discreditable? Isn't it obvious that someone like that — having to deal with other men — was clearly without any experience of human nature? Experience would have taught him the real state of the case: that few are the good, few the evil, and that the great majority are in between.
What do you mean? I said.

I mean, he replied, that you might say of the very large and the very small — nothing is more uncommon than a very large or very small man. This applies generally to all extremes, whether great and small, swift and slow, fair and foul, black and white. Whether you select men, dogs, or anything else, the extremes are few, but there are many in the middle. Have you never noticed this?
Yes, I said, I have.
And don't you imagine, he said, that if there were a competition in evil, the worst would turn out to be very few?
Yes, that is very likely, I said.

Yes, that is very likely, he replied. Although in this respect arguments are unlike men — there you led me on to say more than I had intended. The point of comparison was that when a simple person, with no skill in dialectics, believes an argument to be true which he afterwards imagines to be false — whether it really is false or not — and then another and another, he loses all faith. The great disputers, as you know, come at last to think they have grown to be the wisest of men, because they alone see the utter unsoundness and instability of all arguments — indeed, of all things — which, like the currents in the Euripus, rise and fall in never-ceasing ebb and flow.
That is quite true, I said.

Yes, Phaedo, he replied, and how melancholy — if there is such a thing as truth or certainty or possibility of knowledge — for a man to have lighted upon some argument which at first seemed true and then turned out false, and, instead of blaming himself and his own want of wit, to be so annoyed that he transfers the blame from himself to arguments in general — and forever afterward hates and reviles them, and loses the truth and knowledge of realities.
Yes, indeed, I said, that is very melancholy.

Let us then, in the first place, he said, be careful not to allow or to admit into our souls the notion that there is no health or soundness in any arguments at all. Rather, let us say that we have not yet attained to soundness in ourselves, and that we must struggle manfully and do our best to gain health of mind — you and all other men, with regard to the whole of your future life, and I myself, in the prospect of death. At this very moment, I'm aware that I don't have the temper of a philosopher. Like the common sort of man, I'm only a partisan. Now the partisan, when he's engaged in a dispute, cares nothing about the rights of the question, but is anxious only to convince his hearers of his own assertions. The difference between him and me at this moment is merely this — that whereas he seeks to convince his hearers that what he says is true, I am rather seeking to convince myself; to convince my hearers is a secondary matter with me. And see how much I gain by the argument. If what I say is true, then I do well to be persuaded of the truth. But if there is nothing after death, then at least during the short time that remains I shall not distress my friends with lamentations, and my ignorance will not last but will die with me, so no harm will be done. This is the state of mind, Simmias and Cebes, in which I approach the argument.

And I'd ask you to think of the truth and not of Socrates. Agree with me if I seem to be speaking the truth — and if not, resist me with all your might, so that I don't deceive you along with myself in my enthusiasm, and like the bee, leave my sting in you before I die.
