And now let's proceed, he said. First, let me be sure I have in mind what you were saying. Simmias, if I remember rightly, has fears and misgivings about whether the soul — although a fairer and more divine thing than the body, being in the form of harmony — may not perish first. Cebes, on the other hand, appeared to grant that the soul was more lasting than the body, but he said that no one could know whether the soul, after wearing out many bodies, might not perish herself and leave her last body behind. That would be death — which is the destruction not of the body but of the soul, since in the body the work of destruction is always going on. Aren't these, Simmias and Cebes, the points we have to consider?
They both agreed to this statement of them.
He went on: And did you deny the force of the whole preceding argument, or only part of it?
Only part, they replied.

And what did you think, he said, of that part of the argument in which we said that knowledge is recollection, and therefore inferred that the soul must have existed somewhere else before she was enclosed in the body?

Cebes said he had been wonderfully impressed by that part of the argument, and that his conviction remained absolutely unshaken. Simmias agreed, and added that he himself could scarcely imagine ever thinking otherwise.

But, Socrates replied, you'll have to think otherwise, my Theban friend, if you still maintain that harmony is a compound, and that the soul is a harmony made out of strings set in the frame of the body — because you'd surely never allow yourself to say that a harmony is prior to the elements that compose it.
Never, Socrates.

But don't you see that this is what you imply when you say that the soul existed before she took the form and body of man, and was made up of elements that as yet had no existence? For harmony is not like the soul, as you suppose. First the lyre, and the strings, and the sounds exist in a state of discord, and then harmony is made last of all — and perishes first. How can such a notion of the soul as this agree with the other?
Not at all, replied Simmias.
And yet, he said, there surely ought to be harmony in a discourse of which harmony is the theme.
There ought to be, replied Simmias.
But there is no harmony, he said, between the two propositions — that knowledge is recollection, and that the soul is a harmony. Which of them will you keep?

I think, he replied, that I have a much stronger faith, Socrates, in the first — which has been fully demonstrated to me — than in the latter, which has not been demonstrated at all, but rests only on probable and plausible grounds, and is therefore believed by the many. I know well enough that these arguments from probabilities are impostors, and unless great caution is observed in using them, they are apt to be deceptive — in geometry, and in other things too. But the doctrine of knowledge and recollection has been proven to me on trustworthy grounds — the proof being that the soul must have existed before she came into the body, because to her belongs the essence of which the very name implies existence. Having rightly accepted this conclusion, as I'm convinced, and on sufficient grounds, I must, as I suppose, give up arguing, or allowing others to argue, that the soul is a harmony.
Let me put the matter, Simmias, he said, from another angle. Do you imagine that a harmony — or any other composition — can be in a state other than that of the elements from which it's compounded?
Certainly not.
Or can it do or suffer anything other than what they do or suffer?
He agreed.
Then a harmony does not, properly speaking, lead the parts or elements that make it up, but only follows them.
He assented.
For harmony cannot possibly have any motion, or sound, or other quality which is opposed to its parts.
That would be impossible, he replied.
And doesn't the nature of every harmony depend on the way its elements are harmonized?
I don't follow you, he said.

I mean that a harmony admits of degrees, and is more of a harmony, and more completely a harmony, when more truly and fully harmonized, to any extent that is possible; and less of a harmony, and less completely a harmony, when less truly and fully harmonized.
True.
But does the soul admit of degrees? Is one soul even in the least degree more or less, or more or less completely, a soul than another?
Not in the least.
Yet surely, of two souls, one is said to have intelligence and virtue, and to be good, and the other to have folly and vice, and to be an evil soul — and this is said truly?
Yes, truly.

But what will those who maintain that the soul is a harmony say about this presence of virtue and vice in the soul? Will they say that here is another harmony, and another discord — that the virtuous soul is harmonized, and being herself a harmony has another harmony within her, and that the vicious soul is inharmonical and has no harmony within her?
I can't tell, replied Simmias. But I suppose something of the sort would be asserted by those who say that the soul is a harmony.
And we have already admitted that no soul is more a soul than another — which is equivalent to admitting that a harmony is not more or less a harmony, or more or less completely a harmony?
Quite true.
And that which is not more or less a harmony is not more or less harmonized?
True.
And that which is not more or less harmonized cannot have more or less of harmony, but only an equal harmony?
Yes, an equal harmony.
Then one soul, not being more or less absolutely a soul than another, is not more or less harmonized?
Exactly.
And therefore has neither more nor less of discord, nor yet of harmony?
She has not.
And having neither more nor less of harmony or of discord, one soul has no more vice or virtue than another — if vice is discord and virtue harmony?
Not at all more.
Or, speaking more correctly, Simmias, the soul, if she is a harmony, will never have any vice. Because a harmony, being absolutely a harmony, has no part in the inharmonical.
No.
And therefore a soul, being absolutely a soul, has no vice?
How can she, if the previous argument holds?
Then, if all souls are by their nature equally souls, all souls of all living creatures will be equally good?
I agree with you, Socrates, he said.
And can all this be true, do you think? he said — because these are the consequences that seem to follow from the assumption that the soul is a harmony.
It cannot be true.
Once more, he said — what ruler is there of the elements of human nature other than the soul, and especially the wise soul? Do you know of any?
Indeed, I do not.

And is the soul in agreement with the affections of the body? Or is she at variance with them? For example, when the body is hot and thirsty, doesn't the soul incline us against drinking? And when the body is hungry, against eating? And this is only one instance out of ten thousand of the opposition between soul and body.
Very true.

But we have already acknowledged that the soul, being a harmony, can never utter a note at variance with the tensions and relaxations and vibrations and other affections of the strings out of which she is composed — she can only follow, she cannot lead them.
It must be so, he replied.

And yet don't we now find the soul doing the exact opposite — leading the elements of which she is supposed to be composed, almost always opposing and coercing them in all sorts of ways throughout life? Sometimes more violently, with the pains of medicine and gymnastic; then again more gently. Now threatening, now admonishing the desires, passions, and fears, as if talking to something that is not herself — as Homer in the Odyssey represents Odysseus doing, in the words:
'He beat his breast, and thus reproached his heart: Endure, my heart; far worse hast thou endured!'

Do you think Homer wrote this with the idea that the soul is a harmony capable of being led by the affections of the body, and not rather something of a nature that should lead and master them — herself a far more divine thing than any harmony?
Yes, Socrates, I quite think so.
Then, my friend, we can never be right in saying that the soul is a harmony — for we'd contradict the divine Homer, and contradict ourselves.
True, he said.
So much, said Socrates, for Harmonia, your Theban goddess, who has graciously yielded to us. But what shall I say, Cebes, to her husband Cadmus, and how shall I make peace with him?

I think you'll find a way to propitiate him, said Cebes. I'm sure you've put the argument against Harmonia in a way I never could have expected. When Simmias was mentioning his difficulty, I quite thought no answer could be given to him. So I was surprised to find that his argument couldn't sustain the first onset of yours, and it's not impossible that the other one — Cadmus, as you call him — may share a similar fate.

No, my good friend, said Socrates — let's not boast, lest some evil eye put to flight the words I am about to speak. Leave that, however, in the hands of those above, while I draw near in Homeric fashion and try the mettle of your words. Here's the point: You want it proven to you that the soul is imperishable and immortal. The philosopher who is confident in the face of death appears to you to have only a vain and foolish confidence, if he believes he will fare better in the world below than someone who has led another sort of life — unless he can prove this. And you say that demonstrating the strength and divinity of the soul, and her existence before our becoming men, doesn't necessarily imply her immortality. Granting the soul to be long-lived, and to have known and done much in a former state, still she is not on that account immortal. Her entrance into the human form may be a sort of disease — the beginning of dissolution — which may at last, after the toils of life are over, end in what is called death. And whether the soul enters into the body once only, or many times, makes no difference, you say, to the fears of individuals. Any man who is not devoid of sense must fear, if he has no knowledge and can give no account of the soul's immortality.
This, or something like this, I suspect to be your notion, Cebes. And I deliberately return to it so that nothing may escape us, and so that you may, if you wish, add or subtract anything.
But, said Cebes, as far as I can see at present, I have nothing to add or subtract. I mean just what you say that I mean.

Socrates paused awhile and seemed to be absorbed in reflection. At length he said: You are raising a tremendous question, Cebes — one that involves the whole nature of generation and corruption. If you like, I'll tell you my own experience with it, and if anything I say is likely to help toward solving your difficulty, you may make use of it.
I should very much like, said Cebes, to hear what you have to say.

Then I'll tell you, said Socrates. When I was young, Cebes, I had a prodigious desire to know the branch of philosophy called the investigation of nature — to know the causes of things, why a thing is, and why it is created or destroyed — it appeared to me to be a lofty profession. And I was always agitating myself with considerations such as these: Is the growth of animals the result of some decay which the hot and cold principle contracts, as some have said? Is blood the element with which we think, or is it air, or fire? Or perhaps none of the above — maybe the brain is the originating power of the perceptions of hearing, sight, and smell, and memory and opinion come from them, and science is based on memory and opinion when they have attained fixity. And then I went on to examine the corruption of them, and then to the things of heaven and earth. At last I concluded that I was utterly and absolutely incapable of these inquiries, as I'll satisfactorily prove to you.

I was so fascinated by them that my eyes grew blind to things I had previously thought I — and others — knew quite well. I forgot what I had before taken to be self-evident truths. For example, the fact that the growth of man is the result of eating and drinking — because when by the digestion of food, flesh is added to flesh and bone to bone, and whenever there is an aggregation of congenial elements, the lesser bulk becomes larger and the small man becomes great. Wasn't that a reasonable notion?
Yes, said Cebes, I think so.

Well, but let me tell you something more. There was a time when I thought I understood the meaning of greater and less pretty well. When I saw a great man standing by a little one, I fancied that one was taller than the other by a head. Or one horse would appear to be greater than another horse. And still more clearly did I seem to perceive that ten is two more than eight, and that two cubits are more than one cubit, because two is the double of one.
And what is your notion of such matters now? said Cebes.

I'm far from imagining, he replied, that I know the cause of any of them — by heaven I am. I cannot satisfy myself that when one is added to one, the one to which the addition is made becomes two, or that the two units added together make two by reason of the addition. I cannot understand how, when separated from each other, each was one and not two, and now, when they are brought together, the mere juxtaposition or meeting of them should be the cause of their becoming two. Nor can I understand how the division of one is the way to make two — because then a different cause would produce the same effect. In the former instance, the addition and juxtaposition of one to one was the cause of two; in this, the separation and subtraction of one from the other would be the cause. Nor am I any longer satisfied that I understand the reason why one — or anything else — is either generated or destroyed, or is at all. I have in mind some confused notion of a new method, and I can never accept the other.

Then I heard someone reading, as he said, from a book of Anaxagoras, that mind was the disposer and cause of all. I was delighted at this notion, which seemed quite admirable, and I said to myself: If mind is the disposer, then mind will dispose all for the best, putting each particular in the best place. I argued that if anyone wanted to find out the cause of the generation, destruction, or existence of anything, he must find out what state of being, or doing, or suffering was best for that thing. Therefore a man had only to consider what was best for himself and for others, and then he'd also know what was worse, since the same science comprehends both. I rejoiced to think that I had found in Anaxagoras a teacher of the causes of existence such as I desired, and I imagined he would tell me first whether the earth is flat or round — and whichever was true, he'd go on to explain the cause and necessity of this being so, and then he'd teach me the nature of the best, showing that this was best. If he said the earth was in the center, he would further explain that this position was the best, and I'd be satisfied with that explanation and not want any other kind of cause. I thought I'd then go on and ask him about the sun and moon and stars, and that he'd explain their comparative swiftness, and their returnings and various states, active and passive, and how all of them were for the best.

I couldn't imagine that when he spoke of mind as the disposer of them, he would give any other account of their being as they are, except that this was best. I thought that when he had explained to me in detail the cause of each and the cause of all, he would go on to explain what was best for each and what was good for all. These hopes I wouldn't have sold for a large sum of money. I seized the books and read them as fast as I could, in my eagerness to know the better and the worse.

What expectations I had formed — and how grievously I was disappointed! As I went on, I found my philosopher altogether forsaking mind, or any other principle of order, and having recourse instead to air, and ether, and water, and other eccentricities.

I might compare him to a person who began by maintaining generally that mind is the cause of the actions of Socrates, but who, when he tried to explain the causes of my several actions in detail, went on to show that I sit here because my body is made up of bones and muscles — the bones, as he would say, are hard and have joints that divide them, and the muscles are elastic and cover the bones, which also have a covering or environment of flesh and skin that contains them. As the bones are lifted at their joints by the contraction or relaxation of the muscles, I'm able to bend my limbs — and that's why I'm sitting here in a curved posture. That's what he'd say. And he'd have a similar explanation for my talking to you, which he would attribute to sound, and air, and hearing — he'd assign ten thousand other causes of the same sort, forgetting to mention the true cause: that the Athenians have thought fit to condemn me, and that I've accordingly thought it better and more right to remain here and undergo my sentence. I'm inclined to think that these muscles and bones of mine would have gone off long ago to Megara or Boeotia — by the dog they would — if they had been moved only by their own idea of what was best, and if I had not chosen the better and nobler part of enduring whatever punishment the state inflicts, instead of playing truant and running away. There is surely a strange confusion of causes and conditions in all this.

It may be said, indeed, that without bones and muscles and the other parts of the body, I could not execute my purposes. But to say that I do what I do because of them — and that this is the way mind acts, and not from the choice of what is best — is a very careless and idle way of speaking. I marvel that they cannot distinguish the cause from the condition, which the many, groping about in the dark, are always mistaking and misnaming. Thus one man makes a vortex all around and steadies the earth by the heavens; another gives the air as a support to the earth, which is a sort of broad trough. Any power which, in arranging them as they are, arranges them for the best, never enters into their minds. Instead of finding any superior strength in it, they rather expect to discover another Atlas of the world who is stronger, more everlasting, and more containing than the good. They think nothing of the obligatory and containing power of the good — and yet this is the principle I would gladly learn, if anyone would teach me. But since I have failed either to discover the nature of the best myself, or to learn it from anyone else, I'll show you, if you like, what I have found to be the second-best mode of inquiring into the cause.
I should very much like to hear, he replied.

Socrates proceeded: I thought that, having failed in the contemplation of true existence, I ought to be careful not to lose the eye of my soul — as people may injure their bodily eyesight by observing and gazing at the sun during an eclipse, unless they take the precaution of only looking at the image reflected in water or some similar medium. So in my own case, I was afraid my soul might be blinded altogether if I looked at things with my eyes, or tried to apprehend them by the help of the senses. I thought I had better have recourse to the world of mind and seek there the truth of existence. I dare say the simile isn't perfect — I'm very far from admitting that someone who contemplates existences through the medium of thought sees them only 'through a glass darkly,' any more than someone who considers them in action and operation. However, this was the method I adopted: I first assumed some principle I judged to be the strongest, and then I affirmed as true whatever seemed to agree with this, whether relating to the cause or to anything else, and regarded as untrue whatever disagreed with it. But I'd like to explain my meaning more clearly, because I don't think you understand me yet.
No indeed, replied Cebes, not very well.

There is nothing new, he said, in what I'm about to tell you — only what I have been always and everywhere repeating, in our previous discussion and on other occasions. I want to show you the nature of that cause which has occupied my thoughts. I'll have to go back to those familiar words which are in everyone's mouth, and first of all assume that there is an absolute beauty and goodness and greatness, and the like. Grant me this, and I hope to be able to show you the nature of the cause, and to prove the immortality of the soul.
Cebes said: You may proceed at once with the proof — I grant you this.

Well, he said, then I'd like to know whether you agree with me in the next step. I can't help thinking that if there is anything beautiful other than absolute beauty — if there is such a thing — it can only be beautiful insofar as it partakes of absolute beauty. And I'd say the same of everything. Do you agree with this notion of the cause?
Yes, he said, I agree.

He went on: I know nothing and can understand nothing of any of those other wise causes that are alleged. And if someone says to me that the bloom of color, or form, or anything of that kind, is the source of beauty, I leave all that alone — such talk only confuses me. Simply and singly, and perhaps foolishly, I hold and am assured in my own mind that nothing makes a thing beautiful except the presence and participation of beauty in whatever way or manner obtained. As to the manner I am uncertain, but I stoutly contend that by beauty beautiful things become beautiful. This seems to me the safest answer I can give, either to myself or to anyone else. To this I cling, in the persuasion that this principle will never be overthrown, and that to myself or to anyone who asks the question I may safely reply: That by beauty beautiful things become beautiful. Don't you agree with me?
I do.
And that it is by greatness only that great things become great and greater greater, and by smallness that the less become less?
True.

Then if someone were to remark that A is taller than B by a head, and B less than A by a head, you'd refuse to admit his statement, and would stoutly insist that what you mean is only that the greater is greater by, and by reason of, greatness, and the less is less only by, and by reason of, smallness. Thus you'd avoid the danger of saying that the greater is greater, and the less less, by the measure of the head — which is the same in both — and you'd also avoid the monstrous absurdity of supposing that the greater man is greater by reason of the head, which is small. You'd be afraid to draw such an inference, wouldn't you?
Indeed, I should, said Cebes, laughing.

In the same way, you wouldn't say that ten exceeds eight by, and by reason of, two — you'd say by, and by reason of, number. Or that two cubits exceed one cubit not by a half, but by magnitude — because there's the same liability to error in all these cases.
Very true, he said.

Again, wouldn't you be cautious of affirming that the addition of one to one, or the division of one, is the cause of two? You would loudly insist that you know of no way anything comes into existence except by participation in its own proper essence. Consequently, so far as you know, the only cause of two is the participation in duality — this is the way to make two — and the participation in one is the way to make one. You'd say: I'll let alone puzzles of division and addition — wiser heads than mine may answer them. Inexperienced as I am, and ready to start at my own shadow, as the proverb goes, I cannot afford to give up the sure ground of a principle. And if anyone attacks you there, you wouldn't mind him, or answer him, until you had seen whether the consequences that follow from it agree with one another or not. And when you were further required to give an explanation of this principle, you'd go on to assume a higher principle, and a higher one, until you found a resting-place in the best of the higher principles. But you wouldn't confuse the principle and the consequences in your reasoning, like the Eristics do — at least not if you wanted to discover real existence. It doesn't matter to them, because they never care or think about the matter at all — they have the wit to be well pleased with themselves, however great the turmoil of their ideas. But you, if you are a philosopher, will certainly do as I say.
What you say is most true, said Simmias and Cebes, both speaking at once.
ECHECRATES: Yes, Phaedo — and I don't wonder at their assenting. Anyone with the least sense will acknowledge the wonderful clearness of Socrates's reasoning.
PHAEDO: Certainly, Echecrates — and such was the feeling of the whole company at the time.
ECHECRATES: Yes, and equally of those of us who were not of the company, and are now listening to your account. But what followed?
PHAEDO: After all this had been admitted, and they had agreed that ideas exist and that other things participate in them and derive their names from them, Socrates, if I remember rightly, said:
This is your way of speaking. And yet when you say that Simmias is greater than Socrates and less than Phaedo, don't you predicate of Simmias both greatness and smallness?
Yes, I do.

But still you grant that Simmias does not really exceed Socrates because he is Simmias, as the words might seem to imply — but by reason of the size he has. Just as Simmias does not exceed Socrates because Simmias is Simmias, any more than because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness compared with the greatness of Simmias.
True.
And if Phaedo exceeds him in size, this is not because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has greatness relative to Simmias, who is comparatively smaller?
That is true.

And so Simmias is called both great and small, because he is in a mean between them — exceeding the smallness of the one by his greatness, and allowing the greatness of the other to exceed his smallness. He added, laughing, I'm speaking like a book — but I believe what I'm saying is true.
Simmias assented.

I speak as I do because I want you to agree with me — not only that absolute greatness will never be great and also small, but that greatness in us, or in the concrete, will never admit the small, or admit of being exceeded. Instead of this, one of two things will happen: either the greater will fly or retire before the opposite, which is the less, or at the approach of the less it will have already ceased to exist. But it will not, if it allowed or admitted smallness, be changed by that — even as I, having received and admitted smallness when compared with Simmias, remain just as I was, and am the same small person. As the idea of greatness cannot condescend ever to be or become small, in the same way the smallness in us cannot be or become great. Nor can any other opposite, while remaining the same, ever be or become its own opposite — it either passes away or perishes in the change.
That, replied Cebes, is exactly my notion.

At this, one of the company — I don't exactly remember which — said: In heaven's name, isn't this the direct contrary of what was admitted before — that out of the greater came the less, and out of the less the greater, and that opposites were simply generated from opposites? But now this principle seems to be utterly denied.

Socrates inclined his head to the speaker and listened. I like your courage, he said, in reminding us of this. But you haven't noticed that there's a difference in the two cases. Then we were speaking of opposites in the concrete, and now of the essential opposite which, as is affirmed, neither in us nor in nature can ever be at variance with itself. Then, my friend, we were speaking of things in which opposites are inherent, and which are called after them; now we're speaking about the opposites which are inherent in them and which give their name to them. These essential opposites will never, as we maintain, admit of generation into or out of one another. At the same time, turning to Cebes, he said: Are you at all disconcerted, Cebes, at our friend's objection?
No, I don't feel so, said Cebes — and yet I can't deny that I'm often disturbed by objections.
Then we are agreed after all, said Socrates, that the opposite will never in any case be opposed to itself?
To that we are quite agreed, he replied.
Yet once more, let me ask you to consider the question from another angle, and see whether you agree with me: There is a thing which you call heat, and another thing which you call cold?
Certainly.
But are they the same as fire and snow?
Most assuredly not.
Heat is something different from fire, and cold is not the same as snow?
Yes.

And yet you will surely admit that when snow, as was said before, is under the influence of heat, they will not remain snow and heat — at the advance of the heat, the snow will either retire or perish?
Very true, he replied.
And the fire too, at the advance of cold, will either retire or perish — and when the fire is under the influence of cold, they will not remain as before, fire and cold.
That is true, he said.

And in some cases the name of the idea is not only attached to the idea in an eternal connection, but anything else which — not being the idea — exists only in the form of the idea, may also lay claim to that name. I'll try to make this clearer by an example. The odd number is always called by the name of odd?
Very true.

But is this the only thing which is called odd? Are there not other things which have their own name, and yet are called odd, because — although not the same as oddness — they are never without oddness? That is what I mean to ask: aren't numbers such as the number three of the class of odd? There are many other examples. Wouldn't you say, for instance, that three may be called by its proper name, and also be called odd — which is not the same as three? And this may be said not only of three but also of five, and of every alternate number. Each of them, without being oddness, is odd. And in the same way, two and four and the other series of alternate numbers — every one of them is even, without being evenness. Do you agree?
Of course.

Then now note the point I'm aiming at: not only do essential opposites exclude one another, but concrete things which — although not in themselves opposed — contain opposites, these also reject the idea which is opposed to that which is contained in them, and when it approaches them, they either perish or withdraw. For example: Won't the number three endure annihilation, or anything else, sooner than be converted into an even number while remaining three?
Very true, said Cebes.
And yet, he said, the number two is certainly not opposed to the number three?
It is not.
Then not only do opposite ideas repel the advance of one another, but there are other natures too that repel the approach of opposites.
Very true, he said.
Suppose, he said, that we try, if possible, to determine what these are.
By all means.
Aren't they, Cebes, things that compel whatever they take possession of, not only to take their own form, but also the form of some opposite?
What do you mean?
I mean, as I was just saying, and as I'm sure you know, that those things possessed by the number three must not only be three in number, but also odd.
Quite true.
And on this oddness, of which the number three has the impress, the opposite idea will never intrude?
No.
And this impress was given by the odd principle?
Yes.
And the odd is opposed to the even?
True.
Then the idea of the even number will never arrive at three?
No.
Then three has no part in the even?
None.
Then the triad — the number three — is uneven?
Very true.

To return, then, to my distinction of natures which are not opposed, and yet do not admit opposites — as in the example given, three, although not opposed to the even, does not any the more admit of the even, but always brings the opposite into play on the other side. Or as two does not receive the odd, or fire the cold. From these examples — and there are many more — you may perhaps be able to arrive at the general conclusion that not only will opposites not receive opposites, but also that nothing which brings the opposite will admit the opposite of what it brings, in that to which it is brought. And here let me recapitulate — there's no harm in repetition. The number five will not admit the nature of the even, any more than ten, which is the double of five, will admit the nature of the odd. The double has another opposite, and is not strictly opposed to the odd, but nevertheless rejects the odd altogether. Nor, again, will parts in the ratio three-to-two, nor any fraction in which there is a half, nor, again, in which there is a third, admit the notion of the whole — although they are not opposed to the whole. You'll agree?
Yes, he said, I entirely agree and go along with you in that.

And now, he said, let's begin again. And don't answer my question in the words in which I ask it. Let me have not the old safe answer I spoke of first, but another equally safe one, whose truth will be inferred by you from what has just been said. I mean that if someone asks you 'what that is, the inherence of which makes the body hot,' you'll reply not 'heat' — that's what I call the safe and stupid answer — but 'fire,' a far superior answer, which we are now in a position to give. Or if someone asks 'why is a body diseased?' you'll not say 'from disease,' but 'from fever.' And instead of saying that oddness is the cause of odd numbers, you'll say that the monad is the cause of them. And so with things in general — I dare say you'll understand sufficiently without my giving any more examples.
Yes, he said, I quite understand you.
Tell me, then, what is that of which the inherence will render the body alive?
The soul, he replied.
And is this always the case?
Yes, of course, he said.
Then whatever the soul possesses, to that she comes bearing life?
Yes, certainly.
And is there any opposite to life?
There is, he said.
And what is that?
Death.
Then the soul, as has been acknowledged, will never receive the opposite of what she brings.
Impossible, replied Cebes.
And now, he said, what did we just now call that principle which repels the even?
The odd.
And that principle which repels the musical, or the just?
The unmusical, he said, and the unjust.
And what do we call the principle which does not admit of death?
The immortal, he said.
And does the soul admit of death?
No.

chapters.title: The Soul Is Immortal
paragraphs: Then the soul is immortal?
Yes, he said.
And may we say that this has been proven?
Yes, abundantly proven, Socrates, he replied.
Supposing that the odd were imperishable, must not three be imperishable?
Of course.

And if the cold were imperishable, when the warm principle came attacking the snow, mustn't the snow have retired whole and unmelted? It could never have perished, nor could it have remained and admitted the heat?
True, he said.
Again, if the uncooling or warm principle were imperishable, then the fire, when assailed by cold, would not have perished or been extinguished, but would have gone away unaffected?
Certainly, he said.

And the same may be said of the immortal. If the immortal is also imperishable, the soul, when attacked by death, cannot perish — because the preceding argument shows that the soul will not admit of death, or ever be dead, any more than three or the odd number will admit of the even, or fire or the heat in fire will admit of the cold. Yet someone may say: 'But although the odd will not become even at the approach of the even, why may not the odd perish and the even take the place of the odd?' Now to the person who makes this objection, we cannot answer that the odd principle is imperishable — that has not been acknowledged. But if it had been acknowledged, there would have been no difficulty in contending that at the approach of the even, the odd principle and the number three take their departure. The same argument would have held good of fire and heat and any other thing.
Very true.

And the same may be said of the immortal: if the immortal is also imperishable, then the soul will be imperishable as well as immortal. But if not, some other proof of her imperishableness will have to be given.
No other proof is needed, he said. Because if the immortal, being eternal, is liable to perish, then nothing is imperishable.
Yes, replied Socrates — and yet all men will agree that God, and the essential form of life, and the immortal in general, will never perish.
Yes, all men, he said — that is true. And what is more, gods, if I am not mistaken, as well as men.
Seeing then that the immortal is indestructible, mustn't the soul, if she is immortal, also be imperishable?
Most certainly.
Then when death attacks a man, the mortal portion of him may be supposed to die, but the immortal retires at the approach of death and is preserved safe and sound?
True.
Then, Cebes, beyond question, the soul is immortal and imperishable, and our souls will truly exist in another world!

I am convinced, Socrates, said Cebes, and have nothing more to object. But if my friend Simmias, or anyone else, has any further objection to make, he had better speak out and not keep silence — since I don't know to what other occasion he could defer the discussion, if there's anything he wants to say or to have said.

But I have nothing more to say, replied Simmias — nor can I see any reason for doubt after what has been said. Though I still feel and cannot help feeling uncertain in my own mind, when I think of the greatness of the subject and the feebleness of man.

Yes, Simmias, replied Socrates — that is well said. I may add that first principles, even if they appear certain, should be carefully considered. And when they are satisfactorily ascertained, then, with a sort of hesitating confidence in human reason, you may, I think, follow the course of the argument. And if that is plain and clear, there will be no need for any further inquiry.
Very true.

But then, my friends, he said — if the soul really is immortal, what care ought to be taken of her, not only for the portion of time we call life, but for eternity! The danger of neglecting her, from this point of view, does indeed appear to be awful. If death had been the end of all, the wicked would have had a good bargain in dying, because they would have been happily rid not only of their body but of their own evil together with their souls. But now, since the soul is manifestly immortal, there is no release or salvation from evil except the attainment of the highest virtue and wisdom. For the soul, when on her way to the world below, takes nothing with her but nurture and education. These are said either greatly to benefit or greatly to injure the departed, at the very beginning of his journey there.

For after death, as they say, the genius of each individual — to whom he belonged in life — leads him to a certain place where the dead are gathered together, and from which, after judgment has been given, they pass into the world below, following the guide appointed to conduct them from this world to the other. When they have there received their due and remained their time, another guide brings them back again after many revolutions of ages. Now this way to the other world is not, as Aeschylus says in the Telephus, a single and straight path — if that were so, no guide would be needed, because no one could miss it. But there are many partings of the road, and windings, as I infer from the rites and sacrifices offered to the gods below in places where three ways meet on earth.

The wise and orderly soul follows in the straight path and is conscious of her surroundings. But the soul that desires the body, and that, as I was saying before, has long been fluttering about the lifeless frame and the world of sight, is — after many struggles and many sufferings — hardly and with violence carried away by her attendant genius. When she arrives at the place where the other souls are gathered, if she is impure and has done impure deeds — whether foul murders or other crimes which are the brothers of these, and the works of brothers in crime — from that soul everyone flees and turns away. No one will be her companion, no one her guide, but alone she wanders in extremity of evil until certain times are fulfilled. When they are fulfilled, she is borne irresistibly to her own fitting habitation — just as every pure and just soul who has passed through life in the company and under the guidance of the gods has also her own proper home.
Now the earth has many wonderful regions, and is indeed in nature and extent very unlike the notions of geographers — as I believe on the authority of someone who shall be nameless.
What do you mean, Socrates? said Simmias. I have heard many descriptions of the earth myself, but I don't know, and would very much like to know, which of these you put faith in.

And I, Simmias, replied Socrates, if I had the art of Glaucus, would tell you — although I don't know that even the art of Glaucus could prove the truth of my tale, which I myself should never be able to prove, and even if I could, I fear, Simmias, that my life would come to an end before the argument was completed. I may describe to you, however, the form and regions of the earth according to my own conception of them.
That, said Simmias, will be enough.

Well, then, he said, my conviction is that the earth is a round body in the center of the heavens, and therefore has no need of air or any similar force to be a support. It is kept there and prevented from falling or inclining any way by the equability of the surrounding heaven and by her own equipoise. For that which, being in equipoise, is in the center of that which is equably diffused, will not incline any way in any degree, but will always remain in the same state and not deviate. This is my first notion.
Which is surely a correct one, said Simmias.

Also, I believe that the earth is very vast — and that we who dwell in the region extending from the river Phasis to the Pillars of Heracles inhabit a small portion of it, only about the sea, like ants or frogs about a marsh. There are other inhabitants of many other similar places — because everywhere on the face of the earth there are hollows of various forms and sizes, into which the water and the mist and the lower air collect. But the true earth is pure, and is situated in the pure heaven — there are the stars also — and it is the heaven which is commonly spoken of by us as the ether, of which our own earth is the sediment gathering in the hollows beneath. We who live in these hollows are deceived into the notion that we are dwelling above on the surface of the earth — which is just as if a creature at the bottom of the sea were to fancy that he was on the surface of the water, and that the sea was the heaven through which he saw the sun and the other stars, he having never come to the surface because of his feebleness and sluggishness, and having never lifted up his head and seen, nor ever heard from anyone who had seen, how much purer and fairer the world above is than his own. Our case is exactly the same: we are dwelling in a hollow of the earth, and fancy that we are on the surface. The air we call the heaven, and in it we imagine that the stars move.

But the fact is that, owing to our feebleness and sluggishness, we are prevented from reaching the surface of the air. If any man could arrive at the exterior limit, or take the wings of a bird and come to the top, then — like a fish who puts his head out of the water and sees this world — he would see a world beyond. If the nature of man could sustain the sight, he would acknowledge that this other world was the place of the true heaven and the true light and the true earth. For our earth, and the stones, and the entire region around us, are spoilt and corroded — as in the sea all things are corroded by the brine — and there is nothing noble or perfect growing there, but caverns only, and sand, and an endless slough of mud. Even the shore is not to be compared with the fairer sights of this world. And still less is our world to be compared with the other. Of that upper earth which is under the heaven, I can tell you a charming tale, Simmias, which is well worth hearing.
And we, Socrates, replied Simmias, shall be charmed to listen to you.

The tale, my friend, he said, is as follows. In the first place, the earth, when looked at from above, is in appearance streaked like one of those balls that have leather coverings in twelve pieces, and is decked with various colors, of which the colors used by painters on earth are in a sense samples. But there the whole earth is made up of them, and they are brighter far and clearer than ours. There is a purple of wonderful lustre, also the radiance of gold, and the white which is in the earth is whiter than any chalk or snow. Of these and other colors the earth is made up, and they are more numerous and fairer than the eye of man has ever seen. The very hollows — of which I was speaking — filled with air and water, have a color of their own, and are seen like light gleaming amid the diversity of the other colors, so that the whole presents a single and continuous appearance of variety in unity. And in this fair region, everything that grows — trees, and flowers, and fruits — is in a similar degree fairer than anything here. There are hills, too, having stones in them in a similar degree smoother, and more transparent, and fairer in color than our highly-valued emeralds and sardonyxes and jaspers and other gems, which are only minute fragments of them. For there, all the stones are like our precious stones, and fairer still (compare Republic).

The reason is that they are pure, and not, like our precious stones, infected or corroded by the corrupt briny elements that coagulate among us, and which breed foulness and disease both in earth and stones, as well as in animals and plants. They are the jewels of the upper earth, which also shines with gold and silver and the like. They are set in the light of day and are large and abundant and in all places, making the earth a sight to gladden the beholder's eye. And there are animals and men — some in a middle region, others dwelling about the air as we dwell about the sea, others in islands which the air flows round, near the continent. In a word, the air is used by them as water and the sea are used by us, and the ether is to them what the air is to us. Moreover, the temperament of their seasons is such that they have no disease, and live much longer than we do, and have sight and hearing and smell, and all the other senses, in far greater perfection, in the same proportion that air is purer than water or the ether than air. They have temples and sacred places too, in which the gods really dwell, and they hear their voices and receive their answers, and are conscious of them and hold converse with them. They see the sun, moon, and stars as they truly are, and their other blessedness is of a piece with this.

Such is the nature of the whole earth, and of the things around it. There are many regions in the hollows on the face of the globe everywhere, some of them deeper and more extended than the one we inhabit, others deeper but with a narrower opening than ours, and some shallower and also wider. All have numerous perforations, and there are passages, broad and narrow, in the interior of the earth, connecting them with one another. There flows out of and into them, as into basins, a vast tide of water, and huge subterranean streams of perennial rivers, and springs hot and cold, and a great fire, and great rivers of fire, and streams of liquid mud, thin or thick (like the rivers of mud in Sicily, and the lava streams that follow them). The regions about which they happen to flow are filled up with them. And there is a swinging, or see-saw, in the interior of the earth, which moves all this up and down, and is due to the following cause: There is a chasm which is the vastest of them all, and pierces right through the whole earth. This is the chasm which Homer describes in the words:
'Far off, where is the inmost depth beneath the earth;'

and which he in other places, and many other poets, have called Tartarus. The see-saw is caused by the streams flowing into and out of this chasm — and each of them has the nature of the soil through which it flows. The reason the streams are always flowing in and out is that the watery element has no bed or bottom, but is swinging and surging up and down. The surrounding wind and air do the same — they follow the water up and down, hither and thither, over the earth — just as in the act of respiration the air is always in the process of inhalation and exhalation. The wind swinging with the water in and out produces fearful and irresistible blasts. When the waters retire with a rush into the lower parts of the earth, as they are called, they flow through the earth in those regions and fill them up like water raised by a pump. Then, when they leave those regions and rush back here, they again fill the hollows here, and when these are filled, they flow through subterranean channels and find their way to their several places, forming seas, and lakes, and rivers, and springs. From there they again enter the earth, some of them making a long circuit into many lands, others going to a few places and not so distant — and again fall into Tartarus, some at a point a good deal lower than that at which they rose, and others not much lower, but all to some degree lower than the point from which they came.

And some burst forth again on the opposite side, and some on the same side, and some wind around the earth with one or many folds, like the coils of a serpent, and descend as far as they can, but always return and fall into the chasm. The rivers flowing in either direction can descend only to the center and no further — for opposite to the rivers is a precipice.

Now these rivers are many, and mighty, and diverse. There are four principal ones, of which the greatest and outermost is called Oceanus, which flows round the earth in a circle. In the opposite direction flows Acheron, which passes under the earth through desert places into the Acherusian lake. This is the lake to whose shores the souls of the many go when they are dead, and after waiting an appointed time — which is to some a longer, and to some a shorter time — they are sent back to be born again as animals. The third river passes out between the two, and near the place of its outlet pours into a vast region of fire, forming a lake larger than the Mediterranean Sea, boiling with water and mud. Proceeding muddy and turbid, and winding about the earth, it comes, among other places, to the extremities of the Acherusian Lake — but does not mingle with the waters of the lake. After making many coils about the earth, it plunges into Tartarus at a deeper level. This is that Pyriphlegethon, as the stream is called, which throws up jets of fire in different parts of the earth.

The fourth river goes out on the opposite side, and falls first of all into a wild and savage region, all of a dark-blue color, like lapis lazuli. This is the river called the Stygian river, which falls into and forms the Lake Styx. After falling into the lake and receiving strange powers in the waters, it passes under the earth, winding round in the opposite direction, and comes near the Acherusian lake from the opposite side to Pyriphlegethon. The water of this river too mingles with no other, but flows round in a circle and falls into Tartarus over against Pyriphlegethon. The name of the river, as the poets say, is Cocytus.

Such is the nature of the other world. When the dead arrive at the place to which the genius of each severally guides them, first of all, they have sentence passed upon them, according to whether they have lived well and piously or not. Those who appear to have lived neither well nor ill go to the river Acheron, and embarking in any vessels they may find, are carried in them to the lake. There they dwell and are purified of their evil deeds, and having suffered the penalty of the wrongs they have done to others, they are absolved, and receive the rewards of their good deeds, each according to his deserts. But those who appear to be incurable by reason of the greatness of their crimes — who have committed many and terrible deeds of sacrilege, murders foul and violent, or the like — are hurled into Tartarus, which is their suitable destiny, and they never come out.

Those again who have committed crimes which, although great, are not irremediable — who in a moment of anger, for example, have done violence to a father or mother, and have repented for the rest of their lives, or who have taken the life of another under similar extenuating circumstances — these are plunged into Tartarus, the pains of which they are compelled to undergo for a year. But at the end of the year, the wave casts them forth — mere homicides by way of Cocytus, parricides and matricides by Pyriphlegethon — and they are borne to the Acherusian lake, where they lift up their voices and call on the victims they have slain or wronged, to have pity on them, and to be kind to them, and to let them come out into the lake. If they prevail, then they come forth and cease from their troubles — but if not, they are carried back again into Tartarus and from there into the rivers unceasingly, until they obtain mercy from those whom they have wronged. For that is the sentence inflicted upon them by their judges. Those too who have been pre-eminent for holiness of life are released from this earthly prison and go to their pure home, which is above, and dwell in the purer earth. And of these, such as have duly purified themselves with philosophy live henceforth altogether without the body, in mansions fairer still, which may not be described, and of which the time would fail me to tell.
Therefore, Simmias, seeing all these things, what ought we not to do, in order to obtain virtue and wisdom in this life? Fair is the prize, and the hope great!

chapters.title: The Death of Socrates
paragraphs: 'A sensible person shouldn't insist that my description of the soul and her dwelling places is exactly true. But since the soul has been shown to be immortal, they may reasonably believe that something like this is true. The venture of believing is a noble one, and worth comforting ourselves with such words — which is why I've told this long tale. So let a person be of good cheer about their soul, if they've cast aside the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien and harmful, and sought instead the pleasures of knowledge. Let them adorn the soul with her own proper jewels — temperance, justice, courage, nobility, and truth. So adorned, she's ready for the journey to the world below when her time comes. You, Simmias and Cebes, and all others, will depart at some point. But me — as the tragic poet might say — the voice of fate is already calling. Soon I must drink the poison. I think I'd better bathe first, to spare the women the trouble of washing my body after I'm dead.'
When he'd finished speaking, Crito said: 'Do you have any instructions for us, Socrates? Anything about your children, or anything else we can do for you?'

'Nothing special, Crito,' he replied. 'Just what I've always told you: take care of yourselves. That's the greatest service you can render to me and mine and to all of us, whether you promise it now or not. But if you neglect yourselves and refuse to live by the principles I've laid out — not just today, but always — then no amount of promises will help.'
'We'll do our best,' said Crito. 'But how shall we bury you?'

'However you like — but you'll have to catch me first and make sure I don't slip away!' Then, turning to us with a smile: 'I can't convince Crito that I am the Socrates who has been talking and arguing with you. He thinks I'm that other Socrates — the dead body he'll see shortly — and asks how to bury me. Despite everything I've said about going to the joys of the blessed after drinking the poison, my words seem to have had no effect on Crito. So I need you to guarantee him — as he guaranteed me at the trial. He promised the judges I would stay. You must promise him I won't stay, but will go away and depart. Then he'll suffer less at my death and won't grieve when he sees my body being burned or buried. Don't let him say at the funeral, "Here we lay out Socrates," or "Here we follow him to the grave." Such false words are not only wrong in themselves — they infect the soul with evil. Be of good cheer, dear Crito, and say that you are burying my body only. Do with it whatever is customary, and whatever you think best.'

After saying this, he got up and went to another room to bathe. Crito followed; he told us to wait. So we stayed behind, talking about what we'd heard and reflecting on the enormity of our loss. He was like a father being taken from us, and we were about to spend the rest of our lives as orphans. After the bath, his children were brought to him — two young sons and an older one — and the women of his family came too. He spoke with them, gave them some instructions in Crito's presence, then sent them away and returned to us.

It was now near sunset — he'd been inside a long time. He sat down with us again after his bath, but little was said. Soon the prison guard — servant of the Eleven — came in and stood by him. 'Socrates,' he said, 'I know you are the noblest, gentlest, and best person who has ever been in this place. I won't blame you for the angry feelings that other men show me when I tell them to drink the poison, as the authorities require. I'm sure you won't be angry with me — others are to blame, not I. So farewell, and try to bear what must be as easily as you can — you know why I've come.' Then, bursting into tears, he turned and went out.

Socrates looked at him and said: 'I return your good wishes, and I'll do as you ask.' Then, turning to us: 'How kind the man is! The whole time I've been here, he's visited me often and talked with me, and been as good to me as anyone could be. And now look how generously he grieves for me. We must do as he says, Crito. Bring the cup, if the poison is ready. If not, have the attendant prepare it.'

'But Socrates,' said Crito, 'the sun is still on the hilltops. I know many men wait until late — after the announcement has been made, they eat, drink, and enjoy the company of those they love. Don't hurry — there's still time.'

'Yes, Crito, the people you describe are right to do that — they think they gain something by the delay. But I'm right not to follow their example. I wouldn't gain anything by drinking the poison a little later. I'd only look foolish in my own eyes, clinging to a life that's already forfeit. Please do as I ask, and don't refuse me.'

Crito signaled to the servant standing nearby. The servant went out, was gone for some time, and returned with the guard carrying the cup of poison. 'You,' said Socrates, 'you're experienced in these things — tell me what to do.' The man answered: 'Just walk around until your legs feel heavy, then lie down. The poison will do its work.' He handed the cup to Socrates, who — in the easiest and gentlest manner, Echecrates, without the slightest fear or change of color or expression, looking the man full in the eyes as was his way — took the cup and said: 'May I pour a libation from this cup to any god? Or is that not allowed?' The man answered: 'We prepare only enough for a single dose, Socrates.' 'I understand,' he said. 'But I may and must pray to the gods that my journey from this world to the next be fortunate. So be it — that is my prayer.' Then, raising the cup to his lips, he drank the poison with perfect calm and cheerfulness. Until that moment, most of us had managed to hold back our tears. But when we saw him drinking — saw that he'd finished — we could control ourselves no longer. In spite of myself, my tears were streaming down. I covered my face and wept — not for him, but for myself, at the thought of losing such a friend.

I wasn't the first to break down. Crito had already gotten up, unable to hold back his tears. And Apollodorus, who had been weeping the whole time, now burst into such loud, passionate sobs that he broke the heart of everyone present. Only Socrates remained calm. 'What is this strange outcry?' he said. 'I sent the women away precisely to prevent this kind of thing. I've been told that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, and have patience.' We were ashamed when we heard him, and held back our tears. He walked about until, as he said, his legs grew heavy, and then he lay on his back, as instructed. The man who had given him the poison checked his feet and legs from time to time. After a while he pressed his foot hard and asked if he could feel it. 'No,' Socrates said. Then the man pressed his legs, and so upward, showing us that he was growing cold and stiff. Socrates felt it himself and said: 'When the cold reaches my heart, that will be the end.' He was growing cold around the midsection when he uncovered his face — he had drawn the cloth over himself — and spoke his last words: 'Crito, I owe a rooster to Asclepius. Will you remember to pay the debt?' 'It shall be paid,' said Crito. 'Is there anything else?' There was no answer. After a moment or two, there was a slight movement. The attendants uncovered him. His eyes were fixed. Crito closed his eyes and mouth.
Such was the end of our friend, Echecrates — a man of whom I may truly say: of all the men of his time that I have known, he was the wisest, the most just, and the best.
